LEOB.MARK
California and Hawaii Masonry has long been served by men who have displayed
outstanding leadership qualities. We have been blessed with Grand Masters who have
not only exhibited these qualities but who have also displayed dignity, kindness,
graciousness, compassion, fairness and, when appropriate, a sense of humor. Such a
Grand Master is Leo B. Mark. He will most certainly be remembered for his warmth
of personality and the manner in which he would extend his hand and say, "Hello, my
name is Leo Mark". Throughout his term of office as Grand Master, his thoughts and
actions were always for the benefit of the Craft and the image of Freemasonry. His
subtle sense of humor was a delight to hear and always came forth when it was needed.
He continually practiced the admonition given in the charge of the Fellowcraft Degree,
"You are to judge with candor, admonish with friendship and reprehend with justice".
Our Grand Master, the first of Chinese ancestry to serve as such, was born on May
6, 1922 in San Francisco. He received his education in the public schools of that city
and upon completing grade school, attended San Francisco City College and San Jose
State University. At the age of22, on May 21, 1944 he married the charming and petite
Lora Moy and from this union five children were born - two boys and three girls. He
served his country in the United States Army during World War II in 1944 and 1945.
His career in law enforcement was with the Santa Clara County District Attorney's
office from which he retired as Chief Investigator.
Leo's Masonic career commenced in 1955 when he received the degrees of
Masonry in San Jose Lodge No. 10, serving as Master of that Lodge in 1964. He has
been a Trustee of his Lodge since 1979. Recognizing his abilities, he was appointed a
Grand Lodge Inspector in 1966 and continued serving in that capacity through October
of 1975, relinquishing that post to accept the appointment as Grand Sword Bearer for
the 1975-1976 Grand Lodge year. He became a member of the By-Laws Committee in
1977, served on the Junior Grand Warden Selection Committee in 1978, the Lodge
Resources Development Committee 1978-1984 and the Leadership Workshop Committee in 1984. Closer to home, he was a member of the San Jose Masonic Temple
Board from 1981 through 1984, serving as Vice President of that Board 1982 through
1984. In Scottish Rite Freemasonry, Leo was also most active, serving as the Venerable
Master of the San Jose Lodge of Perfection in 1968, the Commander of Kadosh in 1974,
the Venerable Master of Kadosh in 1983 and the President of the San Jose Scottish
Rite Foundation in 1984. In 1975 he was coroneted a 33° Honorary. He is a member
of Islam Temple of the Shrine and he and Lora are members of Campbell Chapter,
Order of the Eastern Star.
Leo also is the recipient of the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay.
Our Grand Master has also been active in community service, being the charter
President of the Chinese American Citizens' League of Santa Clara County, a Past
President of the San Jose Chinese Language School, a Past President of the California
District Attorney Investigators' Association and a member of the Advisory Board of
the Santa Clara County Valley Police Academy.

LEO B. MARK
Grand Master
October 15, 1987 - October 12, 1988
111

Elected to the station of Junior Grand Warden in October of 1984, his progress
through the Senior Grand Lodge offices culminated in bis election to the highest
Masonic Office in our Jurisdiction, that of Grand Master, at the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge held in October, 1987.
During bis term of office and as he traveled throughout our Jurisdiction, he
continually stressed the theme he had chosen - "The Time Is Now!", alerting the
Brethren to the problems our Fraternity is experiencing and advising them that nothing
can be accomplished by any Grand Master without the full and complete assistance
and cooperation of the membership. For the most part be received this assistance and
cooperation, and it can be truthfully said that California Masonry has benefitted from
the leadership of Grand Master Leo B. Mark.

The One Hundred Thirty-Ninth Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California comme nced at
9:00 A.M. on Monday, October 10, 1988, A.L. 5988 in the California Masonic Memorial
Temple located in San Francisco, California.
Prior to the opening of Grand Lodge, an Organ recital was presented by Harold
M. Hand, Grand Organist.
The opening session of the Annual Communication was raised by Phil Gerow, Past
Master of San Jose Lodge No. 10, the Lodge of Grand Master Mark. The gavel used
to raise Grand Lodge had been hand-made by Bud Frank. The carved dragon gave l
with ruby eyes had a sounding block centered wiLh black jade. The.jade had been carved
with the Grand Master's emblem and filled with gold. They had been previously
presented to Grand Master Mark at a dinner reception hosted by bis Lodge at the San
fose Scottish Rite Temple. Grand Master Mark used this gavel and sounding block
e.xdusively during the Monday morning session.
Responding to the call of the roll were the following Grand Lodge Officers, elected
and appointed, Past Grand Masters and Past Grand Officers:

NECROL OGY REPORT
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Again we have reached that time when we honor the memory of those Masonic
Brethre n who have departed this life since we last met. Du.ring this year we have lost
four hundred thirty-two members of this Grand Lodge including five Worshipfu l
Masters, two Senior Wardens and two Junior Wardens. The names of all of these
Brothe rs \\ill be inscribed in the printed record of this Annual Communic ation.
So thus it is with our departed Brethren - they now know that the day that is most
feared as being the end of all thing.sis but the birthday of Etemjcy. May their souls find
everlasting peace and happiness in the Heave nly Realm above.
Devotional Prayer:
Great Architect of the Universe, Father of us al~ into Thy hands we commend the
souls of our departed Brothers. Our he arts arc heavy in that we will no longer enjoy
their company. Yet our t eachings inspire our hearts and spirits that our friends are now
Raised in Your Celestial Lodge, that House not made with hands, where You ever
preside and we hope Lo follow, in Your good time. Amen.

Decision No. 1.:-lnterprftation of Section 1292 Regarding Manner of Investment by Committee oh Investments
Section 1238 of the California Masonic Code creates a Grand Lodge Commiuee on Investments empowered to invest the funds of this Grand LOdge, including the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, the various other funds of the
Masonic Homes{ the California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic
Memorial Teml? c, and any other_ e~tity of this Gran4 Lodge, e~ccpt constituent
Lodges, Masonic Temple Assoc iations, and Masonic cemeteries.
Section 1292 mandates the funds of those various entities be. invested by the
Commillee on Investments at least 20% in cash or other liquid and secure assets, up to 20% in evidences ofindebte<lness listed and registered on recognized
exchanges and in preferred stock, and up to 60% in common stocks1 shares of
investment trusts and Building and Loan or Savings and Loan Associations, all
as more specifically set fort h m Section U92 as amended.
The seclions g~vcr.n!ng lhose .investments, do not, however, state, whcthyr
the assets of eacfi md1v1dual entity such as the Grand Lodge, the Masonic
Homes General Fund, the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, the California
Masonic Memoria~ Temple, the California Masonic Foundati.on, a!ld the l.ike
may be "J)O
. oled" with one another for the purpose of complymg with Section
1292 or whether each entity must stand on its own fee t.

I have requested our Committee on Jurisprudence to trace the le~lativc
history o f Section 1292 and, without taking your time to repeat the committee's
report in detail, I inform you that Section 1292 had its origin in the old Ross
Digest and then became a part of the 1956 Code as amended. In particular it
was amended in 1972 with various other legislation adopted to carry out the
recommendations of the In-Depth Study Committee presented at the 1970 and
1971 Annual Communications. It was al that time that the dulies of the Committee on Investments were expanded from investing the funds only of the
Grand Lodge, the Masonic H omes Endowment Fund and the Masonic"Homes,
to all of the various entities that 1 earlier enumerated in this Decision.
I am persuaded that although it was reasonable to interpret the 1956 Code
to allow the Committee on Investments to "pool" the funds of the Grand Lodge,
the Masonic H omes Endowment Fund~ and the various funds of the Masonic
Homes for the purpose of the application of the percentages of investment allowed1 such "p.ooling" was not intended to persist with respect to the funds of
the otncr entitles.
In making my Decision, Tam mindful oftbe tax and other legal implica tions
which may, inJeed, cause a disqualification of one or more of our charitable
cor('.H.orat ions were we to pool the ir funds with other entities, particularly should
all tne ir funds be within the higher risk percentage and the re be a substantial
loss. Nevertheless, I make my Decision independe nt of that consideration and
find that although the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, its general fund,. its
various special funds (unless otherwise controlled by the instruments creating
them) and the various lunds of 0th.er entities such as general funds, scholarship
funds, building funds and the like may be "pooled" within I.he entity itself for the
purpose of the application of Sectio n 1292 governing the percentages of investments, the funds of more than one entity may not be "pooled " with the funds of
another entity. For this reason, it is my Decision that:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Although various fun?s o~ separate. entities such as Grand Lod_ge, the.c
MasoJl!c Home~, the Califorma Masonic Foundation and the California
Ma.some Memorial Te~ple may~ pooled wilhin each those entities for the
purpose <?f the application of Sec~on 1292, no funds of any such entity may be
P,OOled with funds of any othe r entity for the purpose of the appljcation of Section 1292, even though !here be a ~mmon investment committee or board of
trustees empowere.d to invest or reinvest the funds of more than one entity."

Rccommc11datio11 No. 2.-Amcndittg C.M.C. Section 2635
Prior lo the 1986 Annual Communication of thjs Grand Lodge, Section
2635 of the C.M.C. provided that a Mason who applied and was elec1cd sub-

seq_uci:it ~o October 1953 to receive the degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this
Jur~sd1ct1on, shal.1 not ~ply for memt?Crstitp in any prerequisite organization
until he passed hIS proficiency and waited one year.
At the 1986 Annual Communication, the Jurispruden ce Committee
presented the .language to carry out the intent of Grand Master DriskeU's
Recommend ation ~o. 2 entitled "Elimination of One-Year Wailing Period".
This recommenda tion and the language to effectuate it was carried over and
adop_ted at the 1987 ~nnual Commurucati on._S ubs~uently.it was discovered
that madvertantly an unportanl phrase contamed m the original language of
Section 2635 was omitted--that phrase being "subsequent to October IlJ53". As
the law now stands no Master Mason having received his degrees in a Lodge of
this Jurisdiction whether before or after October 1953 may apply to any concordant or appendant body of Masonry unless he has proven his proficiency in
the lecture of the Master Mason Degree regardless of when he received his
degrees.
Since this was not the intent of Grand Master Driskell's Recommendation
which was merely to eliminate the one year waiting period\. I recommend that
the present law be amended to include the original phrase subsequent to October 1953" whkh was omitted from the language adopted by this Grand Lodge
.at the 1987 Annual Communication. Section 2635 would then read in relevant
par~ "i'.'- ~ aso n who has received the Degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this
Junsd1ct1on, subseQueot to October 1953 shall not apply for"... ete.

Recommendation No. 4.-Revision of California Masonic Code
It bas now been thirteen years since our California Masonic Code has undergone a revision and I believe the time has come for a comprehensive review
ancfupdate of this Code.
Our Cod_e should be written in such a manner that the average Lodge ofli9Cr, not hav~ng a legal background,. would be able to understand its meaning
Without requmng legal counsel. Tne task of providing such a Code which
P.r~ols our law m Slmplified language will not be an easy one and I would anllClpate that several years will be required for its completion.
In view of the above I re.commend that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special committee to be known as the "Code Revision Committee" and that
this committee be directed to prepare a new revised Code written in simple understandable language to be presented to this Grand Lodge for consitleration
at a subsequent Annual Communication. I further recommend that appropriate
runding, as determined by the Finance Committee, be allocated for the commencement of this undertaking.

Recommendation No. 5.-Duties of the Grand Lecturer

Recommendation No. 6.-Physical Qualifications

The issue of physical qualifications of applicants for the Degrees of Maso~ in
this Jurisdiction has been one which has plagued this Grand Locb!;e time and time
a~ain. In 1979 our regulations concerning this subject were somewliat modified and
smce that time applicants with physical handicaps have been few in number and there
has been no effect upon the Craft.
As a result, I am of the opinion that there is no valid reason necessitating the prior
approval of the Grand Master for a Lodge to receive the application of an applicant
whose physical defects are not correctable with artificial aids. This should be left to
the sound discretion and good judgment of the Lodge.
It is therefore my recommendation that California Masonic Code Section 2602 be
amended to delete the last paragraph requiring that the Grand Master approve the
reception of applications from applicants whose physical defects cannot be corrected
with artificial aids.

Recommendation No. 7-Proficiencies

Under our present regulations a candidate must pass a satisfactory examination
in open Lodge prior to his being advanced to the next Degree. This examination is
based upon his committing to memory a portion of the lecture given him in each of the
Degrees, the obligations and the modes of recognition.
Statistics reveal that in the twenty month period between January 1, 1987 and
August 31, 1988, 3,193 Entered Apprentic e Degrees were conferred by our Lodges. In
that same period of time 1,668 or 52.2% of these Entered Apprentices, so far, have
failed to advance. My Brethren, this is unacceptable to this Grand Master. Eventually
the majority of those candidates will have their fees and contributions forfeited for
failure to advance and they will be lost to our membership rolls. I suggest that the main
reasons for this are the pressures of every day living. Society has so changed, that the
demands upon one's time have become critical factors. If this be so why not adjust our
ritual to meet this situation head on. Let us remember that it was in our hearts that we
were first prepared to be made Masons and that it is our obliaatiops which make us
Masons.
It is therefore my recommendation that the Committee on Ritual be directed to
prepare new Proficiency Examinations for Advancement in the Entered Apprentic e
and Fellow Craft Degrees as contemplated by Sections 2668 and 2674 of the C.M.C.
and for a Master Mason to apply to receive any Dep-ee in or be initiated into any
organizaiton, the prerequisite of membership wherem is that a person be a Master
Mason so that the Brother need only repeat the obligation and demonstrate the modes
of recognition of the highest degree he has received.
To carry out my intent and in addition to my Recommendation No. 2, Section 2635
of the California Masonic Code needs to be amended to read as follows: "Section 2635.
MEMBER SHIP IN PREREQU ISITE ORGANIZ ATIONS. A Mason who has
received the Degrees of Masonry in a Lodge of this Jurisdiction subsequent to October
1253. shall not apply for nor receive any Degree or be initiated into any organizaiton,
the prerequisi te of membership wherem is that a person be a Master Mason, until he
has given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open Lodge, that hs is proficient and qualified in the obliaatjoo and modes of rec°fnjhop of the Degree of Master
Mason. This section does not apply to organizations w ich do not confer Degrees and
do not have formal initiation ceremonies".

were. to be "pooled" and his decision prohibits the pooling of the funds of one enhty
with the funds of a~y other entity. The prohibition against pooling of funds does not
negate the use of a common investment committet; or board of trustees empowered to
invest or re-invest the funds of more than one enllty.

It is possible that there may .be some tax or legal c~msequences if the. funds of a
tax-exempt entity are pooled for mvestment purposes with the funds o_f a non-exempt
entity. It seems reasonabl~ to expect that tax and other legal experts will study further
the consequences of pooling funds.
Therefore, pending furthe.r study and recommendations it is the opinion of the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes that the Grand Master. P.roperly has
decided that the re should be separation of funds among the several ent1t1es of Grand.
Lodge.
We recommend approval of Grand Master's Decision No. 1.

1he Committee on Policy a11d Genera/ Purposes:
In Decision No. 2, Grand Master Leo B. Mark has determined that the prohibition
011 Sunday meetings does not apply to prerequisite organizations.

Each Masonic Grand Lodge in America is sovereign with respect to Masonic
affairs within its jurisdiction. Thus, every American Grand Lodge ultimately has the
right to regulate the conduct of every Masonic organization within its jurisdiction, both
Craft Lodges and prerequisite organiz.ations. The State of Califorma also has broad
rig)?.ts to regulate the conduct of its citizens but chooses to exercise those rights in only
limited circumstances when deemed necessary for the public good. To what extent as
a matter of policy should we as a Grand Lodge regulate Masonic activities in this
jurisdiction?
Certainly, when an activity would invite the contempt of all right thinking people
toward the fraternity, such conduct should be prohibited. Thus, neither Craft Lodge
nor a prerequisite organization may conduct an illegal gambling enterprise. In addition,
we as a Grand Lodge should and do regulate many aspects of the day-to-day administration of our Craft Lodges so as to bring uniformity of operatioo throughout the
jurisdiction. For example, every Craft Lodge must adopt the uniform set of by-laws.
However, we would not attempt to mandate a uniform set of by-laws for prerequisite
org~zations. Thus, as a matter of policy, this Grand Lodge regulates more activities
of Craft Lodges than it does of prerequisite organizations.

_ls the prohibition against Sunday meetings of sufficient importance that the
prohibition should be applied also to prerequisite organizations? Your Committee
assumes that the prohib1t1on of Section 2054 against Sunday mee.tings results from a
time when "blue" laws were common in America. At one time, it was illegal for any type
of business transaction to occur on a Sunday. For example, "blue" laws once prohibited
stores from opening on Sundays. Section 2054 may have resulted from this prohibition.
However, this profobition no longer applies in this state. Because Sunday meetings of
frater.n al organizations no longer violate the spirit or letter of the law and because.
Americans no longer have a general disregard for business or other nonreligious
activities on Sundays, we see no policy reason to prohibit prerequisite organizations
from holding Sunday Meetings.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee therefore, recommends a •yes" vote
on Grand Master Mark's Decision No. 2.
Decision APPROVED.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
We bcliev-e there are two policy questions before the Grand Lodge as~ res!-1lt of
this R ec.ommendation. First, is there a need for a new Code? And second, ts this the
time for it?

deleting the last paragraph.

36

As to the first question, our Code will always ne.c.d revision. There will always be

room for improvement and conflicts which could be removed That does not mean that
it need to be totally revised and republished. After a Code is approved by this Grand
Lodge, the other legislation enacted at the Session at which it was approved, is not
included and must be contained in a supplement.
.
The Grand Master's Recommendation recognizes a more deeply felt need. There
is a desire on the part of many people to have the Code written "in simple language•.
The theory is that by a substantial effort we could draft the Code so that any layman
could understand it. The desire for such simplicity was communicated to those who
drafted the 1975 revision of the Code.
Many experienced draftsmen not only recognize that as difficult but believe. it is
nearly impossible.
While we recognize the desire for a Code to which an oflice.r can turn to fwd. the
answe r to his every question v.-ithout ever needing to consult someone else, we believe
that is improbable of accomplishment. This is not to say that improvement could not
be made, that some conflicts could not be eliminated.
The second question: Is this the time for total revision? While we a.re not the
financial experts of this Gra~d Lodge.• we can only point to the nu~bcr of peopl~ who
should be involved, the mectmgs requared, the drafting and re-draft mg and the ultimate
cost of re publislting and distributing a new Code.
We belie.ve time rrecedent was set by the timin~ of the preparation public;ation of
our second edition o the Code. The first was publishe-0 in 1956, the second m 1975.
We believe that twe nty year intervals might well be appropriate.
For these reasons, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends
a "No"vote.

alarming facts.

as the. culprit. It is possible that this is the case, but tf so, it would. be nelpful to this
Grand Lodge if the statistics were supported by evidence linking the statistics to the
proficiency re.qui.rements. At this point in time no such evidence has been made
available to us. Absent are the results of a survey, if one has been made, as to the reasons
these candidates have failed to advance. Absent is the report, if one has been received,

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
h• founders

of Freemasonry in California saw a need to provide for the
They envisioned a facility
~:meet that need, and in 1898 the Masonic Home at Decoto became a
reality. The love and care provided to our residen'ts at Union City and
covina has since become a legend.

T re of their dependent elderly and children.

aowever, due to the advances in modern medicine and the increasing age of
our membership, the needs of our dependent elderly continue to grow. Nonresident assistance and the Masonic outreach programs were able to relieve
•uch of this ~emand, but the need to provide residential care for our
elderly has increased over the years. To meet this urgent demand, the
Masons in California and Hawaii began the expansion of our two Homes.
construction started in 1987 to provide facilities for 116 ambulatory

a4ults at the Home for Children in Covina and 120 skilled nursing beds at
Union City.
Never h.a s the need been so eminent and the benefits so vast. The time is
now to renew your couunitment to aid and assist our Masonic family. The
teiiete of Freemasonry cannot be better exemplified than by a 100 percent
dedication to the support of our Masonic Homes. The time is now to pledge
to do our fair share.
The time is now for each of us to pledge 100
percent support of the projects designed for all of us. The Time is Now
to Act!
lilith the aforementioned in mind,

I

Proclaim the Hon·th of May 1988 to be

IQ.SONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
in California and Hawaii, and I invite every Mason to share in the support
of our Masonic Homes EndoWU1ent Pund.

Send in your contributions today. Many Brothers match their dues as
contributions. Let us remember that the opportunity is present to 9ive
throughout the year as memorials to our loved ones.
I therefore direct the Secretary to read this Proclamation at the April
and May Stated Meetings of each Lodge in this Jurisdiction and also that
it be published in 11.ll Lodge bulletins as distributed to each B1e111ber.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudenc e, to which the Report of the Comnuttee Upon
the Formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii was referred, reports as follows:
The Committee Upon the Formation has set forth in its Repo~t plans ~d procedures which, if approved by a majority of the members ~f Lodges m Hawau .and by a
majority of the Lodges in Hawaii, will lead to the formation of a new Masoruc Grand
Lodge in that State.
The plans and procedures proposed in the Report are in conformity with the l~w
of the Grand Lodge of California and should the ~ew Grand Lodge be ~ormed, its
intent to assume exclusive jurisdjction over all Masoruc Lodges and Ma~ns m th~ St~te
of Hawaii is in accordance with the American Doctrine of Exclusive Temtonal
Jurisdiction, likewise a part of the law of this Grand Lodge.
We find that the R esolution as proposed by the Committee is adequate to
authorize the vote of the members of Lodges in Hawaii to be taken.
This Resolution d oes not seek to amend the Constituti?n or the Ord~ances of this
Grand Lodge, and only a majority affirmative vote is reqmred for adoption.

The Committee on Policy and General Pwposes:

.

For more than 20 years, perhaps much longer, there has been a desm; on the part
of a substantial number of the Hawaiian members of this Grand Lodge to form a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii.

It has been the policy of I.his Grand Lodge to aid in the studies of the feasibility of
this and in this way as a practical matter to not discourage the concept. of a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii. The report of the Committee points out the cooperation between
Lhe Lo<lges of Hawaii and this Grand Lodge.
A plan has now been devised which, if the necessary approvals are obt.Uned, wi~
cause the formation of a new Grand Lodge. The creation of a Grand Lodge of Hawau
would be one of the major changes or the century in this Grand Lodge.
We are troubled by several questions? What financial arrangeme,nt will be made
with regard to Hawaiian residents now in California Masonic Homes? Are any other
financial transfers between the two Grand Lodges conte.mplate d or approved?
We are also troubled by the projected per capita assessment as contained in the
proposed budget of the new Grand Lodge.
These are probably among many matters which either have been or will be
considered and addressed.
While future Grand Masters may bemoan the demise of a favored area of inspection, the proposal seems reasonable. Your Committee on Policy and G eneral Purposes
recommends a "Yes• vote, and says, "Aloha".

59

'fhe Committee on Finance:
On the Report of the Special Committee on the Study of the Feasibility of a Grand
Lodge of Hawaii, your Grand Lodge F'manre Committee is of the opinion that the
financial impact on the Grand Lodge of California will be minimal.
It is this Committee's opiruon that the loss of the per capita income generated by
the 2850 Hawaiian Brethre n will be offset by a correspondin g reduction in the expenses
incurred for Grand Master's VISitation, Travel and Ritual for the Hawaiian Lodges
and we therefore offer no recommenda tion on this Re port.

Resolution APPROVED .

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Wor.rhipful Grand Ledge, F. &: A.M. of California:
The financial records of Grand Lodge and its several entities have been examined
by the accounting firm of Lindquist, Von Husen and Joyce verifying the assets,
liabilities, reve nues, support and expenses. SeveraJ reports of the auditors for the fiscal
year ending June 30, 1988, are printed as part of the Grand Treasurer's report and are
available to me mbers of Grand Lodge.
The accounting department of Grand Lodge, cooperating with the Grand
Treasurer, provides an outstanding service in maintaining the accounts of Grand
Lodge, the Masoruc Homes of California, the California Masoruc Foundation, and
California Memorial Temple. Hugo Delfin and the staff provide accurate and comprehensive monthly financial statements in a highly professional manner.
The members of Grand Lodge, like stockholders of a major corPQration, must be
informed on a timely basis as to the financial condition of Grand Lodge and be assured
that reve nues and expenses are kept in balance.
The generositv of California and H awaii Masons and their friends in contributing
fmancially to the Masoruc H omes of California, the Homes Endowment Fund and the
California Masonic Foundation has been outstanding. Even though Lodge membership for the time has been declining our benefactors give assurance to the future of the
Homes and the charitable activities of the Foundation. The California Masonic
Memorial Temple, a Masonic landmark in California, continue.s to thrive because of
the public use and acceptance of its outstanding facilities.
The Grand Treasurer gratefully acknowledges the support of the Grand Master,
G
the rand Secretary, and the accounting staff during his initial year in office.
Respect fully submitted,
Ralph H. Head, Grand Treasurer
Referred to the Commiltee on Distribution. That Committee referred the entire
report of the Grand Treasurer to the Committee on Finance. (The Grand Treasurer's
Report also included copies of the audits of the several Masonic Entities.)

In accordance with various requirements of Section 1108 of the California Masonic

busin~ of the Grand Lodge for the fiscal year ending on June 30, 1988.

Masonic Lodge Scholarship Awards (Resolution No. 87-33, 1987 Proceedings,
page 245.)

Those monies which are due to the Grand Lodge, and which have been collected,
have been paid to the Grand Treasurer and have been credited to the ~ppropriate
accounts. This is reflected in the printed report of the Grand Treasurer which has been
audited by our Certified Public Accountants. Maintained and on file in the accounting
department of the Grand Lodge office are all supporting ledgers, vouchers and
receipts.

Charity Committee to Remit Dues (Resolution No. 87-46, 1987 Proceedings, page
1.62.)

During the past year the usual mee~ of the Boards of Trustees of ~asonic
Homes, the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the California Masomc Foundation were held and the minutes of these mee~ were duly recorded and are on file.
Minutes of mee~ of the Investment, Retirement and Executive Committees were
also duly recorded and these also are on file.
In August of this year the F'mance Committee met with the Executive Committee
and others who are involved with the preparation of the operating budget for the Grand
Lodge for the fiscal year 1988 -1989. During the course of this Annual Communication,
the report and recommendations of the F'lnance Committee will be presented to you.
Once again my appreciation is offered to those with whom our office comes into
contact for their cooperation and understanding. It is truly an example of men of
goodwill working together for the good of Freemasonry.

many retired Masons and Sojourners who no longer feel comfortable in driving long
distances after dark to attend Lodge. They now have thirty-nine prospective members
and a full line of prospective Officers. They anticipate applying for Dispensation early

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Charters:

To the Most Worshipfal Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California

Most Worshipful Grand Master, distinguished guests and Brethren. At our 1987
Annual Communication· we reported to you that three Masonic Clubs were actively
seeking to become Lodges undet:Dispensation. They were Victor Valley Masonic Club
in Victorville, Sunrise Masonic Club in Reseda, and the Temecula Valley Masonic Club
in Temecula. We also reported that on September 9, 1987 the Committee had recommended to Grand Master Levitt that Three Stars Masonic Club in Chula Vista be
granted Dispensation.
·
Three Stars Masonic Club became Three Stars Lodge U.D. on October 3, 1987
when Dispensation Ceremonies were conducted by Grand Master Levitt. Since receiving Dispensation the Lodge has conferred nineteen F'rrst Degrees, eleven Second
Degrees, and Raised eight candidates to Master Mason. Seventeen members have been
received by Affiliation. Since receiving Dispensation Lodge membership has increased
'
from thirty-six to sixty-one members.
On January 28, 1988 the Committee recommended to the Grand Master that
Sunrise Masonic Club be granted Dispensation. On April 5, 1988 Grand Master Mark
conducted Dispensation Ceremonies and Sunrise Masonic Club became Sunrise
Lodge U.D. Since Dispensation the Lodge has received six members by Affiliation,
conferred four F'rrst Degrees, two Second Degrees, and plans to Raise two candidates
to Master Mason this month. Membership has increased from forty to forty-six
members.
The Charters Committee met with representatives of Three Stars Lodge U.D. and
representatives of Sunrise Lodge U.D. on October 9, 1988. Both Lodges have surrendered their Dispensations and submitted their records for our examination as
required by our regulations. We find they meet all of our prerequisites for becoming
Chartered Lodges. It is our recommendation that Charters be granted and numbers

The Temecula Masonic Club in Temecula was formed on July 1, 1987 with the goal
of providing a Lodge in an area where there are many Masons and Sojourners and no
Lodges in the immediate area. Their goal was achieved not by forming a new Lodge
but through cooperation with Catalina Island Lodge No. 524 which moved from
Avalon, Catalina Island to Temecula. The majority of the Temecula Masonic Club
members have Affiliated with Catalina Island Lodge thus giving that Lodge potential
Officers. The principal reason for the Lodge leaving the island was its problem in
obtaining officers.
That portion of the report of the Grand Secretary dealing with Charter changes
has been referred to this Committee for consideration.
·
We find that all requirements of our laws have been complied with, and, therefore
respectfully recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized to properly endorse
the Charters of these named Lodges. Most Worshipful, I now move the adoption of
this recommendation.
On behalf of the Charters Committee, we thank you for the privilege and honor of
serving our great Fraternity this year.
Most Worshipful, I now move the adoption of the total report as presented.
Respectfully submitted,

Adrianus Sneep
Vandell C. Owen
Norbert E. Driggers
Clyde M. Loughead

This past year, for the first time, the Grand Lodge roster and Procee~ were
dcYCioped in-house by the use of a "desk top" publishing program. Certain difficulties
in the use of this program were encountered which had to be overcome and which
accounted for the lateness in distributing the Proceedings in particular. While we are
not entirely satisfied with the format of either the roster or the Proceedings, we would
espect to do a more professional job the next time around. In the meantime I am most
p1Cased to advise you that by developing both of the above stated publications in-house .
byuse of the "desk top" publishing method a net sa~ of$15,716.00was realized. We
baVC recently purchased an optical scanner which will eliminate the need for keyboard
eattYOf data and which will result in even additional cost sa~ as well as time savings.
fJl addition to the roster and Proceedings we have now used the desk top publishing
program for other publications thereby making it even more cost effective.
GOLDEN VETERANS' AWARDS
It would seem that misunderstan~ exist with respect to our Golden Veterans'
Awards Program as to the proper procedures for initiating the award and the follow
through to the presentation. It is most important, once the eligibility date has been
verified by our office, that the recipient be so advised and a presentation date be set
as soon as possible. Once this date has been determined, our office must be so notified
and the certificate and lapel pin will then be forwarded to the Inspector approximately
two weeks prior to that date. Many a recipient has gone to his reward before the
presentation was accomplished merely because an unduly length of time transpired
between the eligibility date and the date finally set for presentation.
MEMBERSHIP
I am sorry to report that our jurisdiction has again suffered a substantial loss in
membership during the year ending on June 30, 1988. A glance at the membership
statistical table included in this report reveals this sad fact. It also reveals the continuing
decline in the number of degrees conferred over the past five years which when
combined with the membership loss paints a rather dismal picture of the future of the
Fraternity in our jurisdiction.
The trend as above described is not confined to our jurisdiction, but may be found
throughout our sister jurisdictions both within the United States and abroad. It will
take our combined efforts and creativeness to slow this trend and eventually to reverse
it. Hopefully this will not be too far into the future. Meanwhile, we must continue to
provide new ideas, new programs and maintain a positive and optimistic attitude.
CONCLUSION
This concludes my eighth annual report as your Grand Secretary. I appreciate the
opportunity of being able to work closely with the various Committees and Boards of
Grand Lodge, the various Lodge officers, the Inspectors, the Executive Committee
and, of course, with those employees who handle the day to day routine business in our
office. It is indeed a pleasureable and rewarding experience and I offer my sincere
thanks to the members of this Grand Lodge to whom I am beholden.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Yoilr Committee on Jurisprudence has reviewed 177 Applications for Dispensation directed to the Grand Master for his approval. Dispensations, as you are aware,
are required to change the dates of Stated M~ hold outdoor Degrees, meet in
buildings other than the one described in your Charter, hold Special Elections,
participate in parades or wear Masonic regalia outside the Lodge Hall, and for other
reasons as more particularly set forth in the California_Masonic Code. We find that
Grand Master Mark has acted properly within his executive powers and Masonic law
in each instance in which he has given his approval.
As is always the case, the Grand Secretary and his staff are of monumental
assistance to the Lodges in making an initial review and, when necessary, requiring
revision of Dispensations prior to submitting them to the Grand Master for his
approval. Next in the procedure is the review and the approval of the Grand Master
to be followed by the further review of this Committee. In some instances, it is necessary
to require further clarification prior to the ultimate approval by the Committee on

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE

Review of the proposed changes with the Grand Secretary in July of 1988 is of
great value in insuring that due form and procedure have been followed.
The Grand Master referred Resolution No. 88-2 to your By-Laws Committee as
it involves a change of Lodge name and resulting change in By-Laws. California
Masonic Code Section 2022 provides that only Grand Lodge can approve a name
change. Therefore, this Committee has no jurisdiction to determine the merits of the
Resolution. Your Committee reviewed the form and procedure and finds sa,me to have
been correctly followed. Based thereon, the By-Laws Committee recommends a "Yes"
vote on Resolution No. 88-2.
Citrol Lodge No. 656 Request for Charity Committee Increase is approved with
notation that the correction does not contain the Seal of Lodge.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1787
Your Committee has considered Application for Restoration in Trial Record
numbered 1787. The former member of Needles Lodge No. 326 has shown sufficient
realization of the circumstances leading to his expulsion. Your Committee is satisfied
with his change of outlook, his rehabilitation, and acceptance of him by his Lodges and
his community. Sufficient time has elapsed since the expulsion in this case to indicate
that these positive factors are not mere temporary changes.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Application for Restoration in Trial Record 1787 be
approved.
Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2256

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2173

In Trial Record No. 2256, a member and Past Master of Ll'bertas-Security Lodge
No. 466 w~ charged with the theft of irrigation pipe having the approximate value of
$33!000.<_JO m 1985. He was found Guilty by Jury of violating Section 487(1) of the
Califorma Penal Code (Grand Theft), a Felony and sentenced to jail and three years
of Proba~on. He was also ordered to make restitution. The Court of Appeal upheld
·
the Verdict.

In Trial Record No. 2173, a former member of Malta Lodge No. (J61, was charged
with a violation of the California Penal Code, in that he molested his stepdaughter, a
child under the age of 18 years. He entered a plea of Not Guilty and a jury trial was
held on May 18, 1978, in which he was found Guilty.

On March 4, 1988, the member was served with Masonic Charges and did not
respond The Trial Master found the member Guilty of the Charges and fixed the
Penalty of Suspension.
Your Tri!l1 Review.Committee concurs with the findings of the Trial Master, but
respectfully disagrees with the Penalty. A review of evidence reveals no mitigating facts.
The. acts of Accused were of sufficient severity that the Penalty should be raised to
Expulsion by the Grand Lodge.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2256 the findings of Guilty of unmasonic
conduct be affirmed, but that the Penalty be raised to Expulsion.
Report ADOPTED.

After the conviction and sentence, which was affirmed on appeal, charges of
11Jl1118SOniC conduct were filed on October 21, 1981. He was found Guilty of unmasonic
conduct and the Penalty was fixed at Expulsion. This was affirmed by Grand Lodge in
0ctober, 1982.
He now seeks Reinstatement and has submitted several letters of personal reference and recommendation. His Lodge has voted to oppose his Restoration.
Your Committee feels that due to the nature of the violation, the relatively short

period of time since it occurred, and the opposition of his own Lodge, we recommend

RESOLVED, that the Petition for Restoration in Trial Record No. 2173 be

Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2289
In Trial Record No. 2289 a member of Moreno Valley No. 804 was charged with
engaging in an ongoing incestuous sexual relationship with his niece, who was a minor.
He entered a plea of Guilty in the Superior Court of the State of Indiana.
On November 30, 1987 the Accused was served with Masonic Charges and did not
respond The Trial Master found the member Guilty of the Charges and fixed the
Penalty of Suspension.
Your Trial Review Committee concurs with the findings of the Trial Master, but
respectfully disagrees with the Penalty. A review of the evidence reveals that the
Accused engaged in sexual intercourse with his niece on numerous occasions over a
long period of time in Indiana. After the Accused came back to California he continued
calling his niece and writing her letters to entice her to come to California.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes that the acts of the Accused are of
sufficient severity that the Penalty should be raised to Expulsion by the Grand Lodge.
We therefore submit the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2289 the findings of Guilty of unmasonic
conduct be affirmed, but that the Penalty be raised to Expulsion.
Report ADOPTED.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 2271
In Trial Record No. 2271, a member of Forest Masonic Lodge No. 130 in the
Jurisdiction of Wisconsin was charged with unmasonic conduct in Apollo-Woodstock
Lodge No. 396 upon two (2) specifications:
F'rrst: That from January through August 1985, he did misappropriate certain
funds,
Second: That from June through August, 1985, he did misappropriate certain
funds.
The accused responded with a plea of Not Guilty and a Trial by Commission was
conducted.
The Lodge elected seven (7) Commissioners and three (3) alternate Commissioners. However, only six (6) Commissioners participated in the Trial and found the
member Guilty upon the specifications of unmasonic conduct and set the penalty at
Expulsion. These charges appear to be well known in the community and have resulted
in great notoriety in the Masonic organizations.
The California Masonic Code, Section 3346, provides that the Lodge shall, by a
vote of the Lodge, determine the number of Commissioners (not less than seven nor
more than nine). Here that procedure was followed with the Lodge voting for seven
(7) Commissioners and three (3) alternates.
In the Trial in the matter, only six (6) Commissioners were present. California
Masonic Code Section 3362 provides in part"...Vacancies on the Commission, because
of objection or otherwise, shall be filled by the remaining Commissioners, subject to
the approval of the Trial Master, from qualified members of the Lodge; provided that

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&.A.M. of California:
Brethren--At the outset, I take this opportunity to express to you, my sincerest
"Thank You"--for the privilege to serve this Grand Lodge as its Grand Lecturer.
In compliance with out statutes, I report to you as follows. All of the ritual has been
reviewed throughout the entire jurisdiction. Conferences were held in each Division,
proving once again the efficiency of our present system of instruction. It is further proof
that the instructive tongue and the attentive ear remain the greatest teaching tools for
the spoken ritual and that seeing and doing beat a textbook any day. The Inspectors of
the seven (7) Divisions performed their assigned portions of the work exceptionally
well and are to be congratulated on it.

Seminars were conducted at random locations in all Divisions for groups of Lodges
and the Brethren at large who wished to attend. These seminars afforded the opportunity for the Grand Lecturer to meet with the Officers and Brethren on a one-on-one
basis and to create a closer relationship with the Lodges. This program was well
received and must be continued and expanded.

The Grand Lecturer of the Grand Lodge of Arizona in 1986 expressed it well when
he cited an old legend, and I quote him, "He spoke of a young lad during the Napoleanic
Wars, a lad too young to fight, who was permitted only to carry the regimental banner.
During one bitter engagement, his unit was advancing on the enemy under heavy fire.
In his youthful zea~ the boy went so far ahead of the regiment, that be was almost out
of contact. The commanding officer sent a runner bearing the message, 'Bring the
standard back to the line.' With heroic recklessness the lad sent back the ringing reply,
'No, no, you bring the line up to the standard.'" In drawing an analogy with modern day
Freemasonry in California, I am induced to believe that the standard bearer was right
and not the commanding officer. We do need to bring the line up to the standard/

Applying for admission into the Masonic Homes is a monumen tal decision
by a Mason or his widow. To some it is a regret for having to leave a home of
many years; to others, a tremendo usly necessary move to find the relief and
solace of freedom from want. That "want" may be a fre.edom from fear; from illness past, present, and future; it may be a freedom from financial worry or a
"want" to be with people. of their own choosing .
In the year 1850, the 69 Master Masons in Sacrame nto gave all of their assets to assist the then ill and dying Masons and their families.
It was then that the 69 Master Masons decided "The Masons of Californi a
must have a facility to care for widows and orphans."
Down through the Jears Masons have been concerne d about such a
Masonic Care Home. To ay, on the beautiful hills of southern Alameda County and in the heart of Southern Californi a in Covina lie two of the most beautiful, modern and efficient structure s to meet that responsib ility. I am well within
the mark when I say there are no such facilities anywhere which exceed the
beauty and effectiven ess of these Homes. NONE! Masons in Californi a should
regularly point with pride to these two magnifice nt Masonic Homes dedicated
to the Brotherly Love we espouse.

for admisi~ necessary to care for the proposed resident until there is a room
sion.
Although the first call on the funds of the Lodge is for the "relief of its own
members1 tneir widows and orphans," the Lodge quite often is without funds to
provide tne needed care.
To assist the Lodge in meetin_g their responsibility, the Masonic Homes
created "Non-Re sident Assistanc e, wherein tlie cost of care pending admission

When and if the applicant is admitted , the Masonic Homes pays all the cost
thereafte r.

During this year, the Personnel Committee conducted their bi-annual review
of the Administrators' recommendations for modifications to all salary ranges.
It is the continuing plan to carefully review these with other similar facilities to
insure an acceptable salary level for every employee.
An industry shortage of Registered and Licensed Nurses has also had an
impact on the Skilled ~ursing Facility at Union City. A careful review of wages
paid to personnel by other Sk:1lled Nursing Facilities and Acute Hospitals in.the
Bay Arca Region was conducted jointly by the Personnel and Budget Committees. Special consideration was given an Registered and Licensed Nursing positions and wages were adjusted to meet the competitive industry levels.

In addition, the Personnel Committee recommended to the Board of Trustees a merit pool for this year's merit increases for deserving employees. The
total merit pool and special salary considerations as outlined received full Board
apprOV,!il. All salary adiustment~ are provided for and are within the approved
Masomc Homes annual Operating Budget.

MASONIC HOME, UNION CITY
1987 - 1988
Another year has passed and to use a much varied phrase, "what goes
around comes around". People's names change, faces change, events change;
but traditions remain and the Masonic Home remains with it's location, it's stature, it's beauty and with pride, it's reputation. As in previous years, I welcome
the opportunity to report about the people and events surrounding the Masonic
Home at Union City.
The many functions scheduled throughout the year would take up too much
space in this report but a large share of them consist of traditional events of
Ions standing. These include the Grand Master's Reception, Grand Lodge
Visitation Day, the Residents' Christmas Party, visitations to the Home by
Lodges and other groups of all description, and visits by the residents to
Masonic affiliated events.
Among the Masonic groups visiting the Home, we counted eighteen
Lodges, five of them who conferred degrees upon their candidates; ei~ht visits
from Chapters of DeMolay; eleven Bethels of Job's Daughters; eight Assemblies of Rainbow Girls; and six Chapters from the Order of Eastern Star. In
addition, two Shrine Clown Units and two of the Shrine Bands made special
visits to entertain the residents.
Our residents have been invited to participate in many traditional Grand
Lodge activities throughout the year both at and away from the Home: A Constitution Observance Dinner hosted by Alameda Lodge No.167; Masonic Family Night in San Jose; Public Schools Week finds the residents actively involved
with local schools;.and of course, the activities of Grand Lodge Week in San
Francisco. Ot:her activities that find the men and women from the Home involved in the community include a variety of events. Among them are: Union
Ciry's Senior Citizen Association, Stanford Universitf Researc~ program, and
a Sign Language class sponsored by one of the loca Commumty Colleges. A
very innovative and rewarding adventure was implemented in cooperation with
Ohlone Community College. An intergenerational program that involves our
residents with young children of some of the adults attending colJege is called
"Grand Pals". The location of the meetings alternates between the Home and
the College and consists of picnics (both indoors and outdoors), games for
youn~ and old, story tellin~ by all participants and refreshments. The objective
of thlS program is to proVtde the children with an understanding of aging and
an "older" grandparent relationship that many of them do not have, as welJ as
give our residents the opportunity to experience the pleasure of an on-going
relationship with preschool children.
As it has been for many years a variety of activities that would please different interests of people took place at the Home. A partial list of the events included the following:
Resident Town Hall Meetings
Pizza Partie.s
Union City Lioness Club Barbeque for residents
Resident Volunteers Banquet
Golden Girl Fashion Show

Wedding Anniversaries of 60 or more years were celebrated by nine

Congratulations to our High-Twelve Club No. 606 for winnin~ th~ Blue Ribbon Award for BEST CLUB BULLETIN at the State Convention m November.
Congratulations were also extended to four of our residents who decided
to be united in marriage. Bro. Robert Wolfenden from Center Lodge No. 465
Fresno and Mrs. Inez Lewis from San Gabriel-Southern California Lodge No.
278 repealed the vows before a Justice of the Peace in Fremont on May 28. And
on June 3, Bro. Thomas HowelL Cahuenga-La Brea Lodge No. 513 and Mrs.
Charlotte Apostel, Starr King Lodge No. 344 were married in the chapel at the
Home.
The two events that have enjoyed the longest traditions took place this year
again and both of them were successfully participated in by residents and visitors
alilc.e. Grand Lodge Visitation Day saw approximately 500 people touring the
Home, having lunch, and enjoying a concert. The other event was held for the
74th time and occured on the third Saturday of August, as it has been for most
of those years. "JAM and JELLY DA y~ was presented by the East Bay Past
Matrons Association and through their efforts, contributed $2,538.00 for the
Home to purchase jams and jellies for the residents.
One of our newer traditions continued this year because our Resident
entertainers known as "The Hilltoppers" were again busy presenting their performance sixteen times. Twelve of them involved traveling away from the Home
to various Masonic and non-Masonic organizations. The other four shows were

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

103

presented at the Home as part of annual events; The Residents' and Employees'
Christmas Parties; and the Grand Master's Reception. A very unique feature
surrounded their performance on February 29 (Leap year) when the Union
City Rotary Club and eleven City officials joined them plus 14 delegates from
our Sister City, Santa Rosalia, Baja California who were here for lunch, a tour,
and a "show". The uniqueness resulted from the necessity to have one of the
visitors translate all the remarks made by the Director, Ruth Brown, which she
makes to introduce the musical numbers.
During this year the operation of the Home remained the same basically,
but new faces joined us to assist in the continuation of presenting quality care
and services to the men and women of the Home. In September we entered into
contract with Morrisons Inc. to manage our Dietary Services and were introduced to Kathy Rush, their Manager designee.
January found us acquiring two new administrative personnel; both of them
are licensed nursing home administrators and have proven to be valuable additions to our staff. Mr. Kelly Wiest filled the position of Assistant Administrator
with responsibilities centered around the Residential Services and Social Services. Mrs. Frances Davis has assumed the role of Associate Administrator and
her duties involve overseeing all of the Health Services. In addition to the above
changes we have a new Accounting Manager, Ralph Campbell.
All of our employees were given recognition by The United Way for our
contributions being increased by one of the largest percenta~es in Alameda
County. A revolving plaque was presented to our Busmess Services Director at
a ceremony in San Francisco. It denotes a growing concern for the welfare of
fellow citizens in our communities and it also reflects the sensitivity to people
and the idea of caring for others. This same attitude is present among the approximately 300 men and women employed at the Home as they carry out their
duties and offer lo~ng care to the residents.
It is my privilege to be on the working end of the tools of Masonry as they
are applied to our brethren, their wives and/or widows. On behalf of all the residents and employees at the Masonic Home in Union City, I offer my sincere
appreciation to every Masonic Brother, members of affiliated organizations,
and friends of the Home in our Grand Lodge for their collective generous support that has enabled this facility to exist and function for the past 89 years.
With an enormous sense of pride and gratitude I THANK YOU.
Respectfully submitted,
J. Burton Brown,Administrator

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR, COVINA HOME
1987 - 1988
It is with not only pleasure but also excitement that this report is made to
the Grand Lodge.
COVINA EXPANSION
This has been a most excitin$ year in Covina. Much has been accomplished
in preparation for the Residential Facility for the Elderly. The basic policies
and procedures have been developed. An application for a facility license has
been submitted to the California Department of Social Services. The facility is
now under construction. Regular inspections are made to assure that the work
proceeds according to the well-considered plans which are attentive to both
strength and ornament.

114

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
Personne l needs are being assessed. Where practical and feasible, proper-

ty and pr0$1'ams will be allocated. This will assure each compone nt to be most

cost effective and efficient. The physical care and supervision rrograms for
Adults and Children will not be commingled. Although, each wil have the opportunity to associate and participa te with one another on a voluntary basis and
thus develop a neighborly, if not fictive, family relationsh ip.
. During an i!1t.erim vacancy in the Assistant Administ rator position al Union
City, your Adrnm1strator was pleased to serve and learn at Union City for a sixmonth yeriod of time. This invaluable experienc e will help in the joint management o the adult and children' s services at Covina.
A ceremony which appropria tely dedicates this expansion program is
planned for Sunday, February 12, 1989 at the Covina Home. I would like to take
this opportun ity to personally invite you to this historical event.
CHILDR EN'S HOME
Our Child Care rrogram, having been reorganized, refined and improved
over the past severa years, is now operating at a most efficient level. Your
Masonic Home continues its service to children in a home-like environment for
children unable to live with their guardians or extended families.
Your Board of Trustees has been most careful and attentive to approve
~nly those apJ?li~ations which qua lify according to admission policies. Applications for adm1ss1on are carefully evaluated to assure that children' s needs can
be met in this Home and there exists no criminal delinquency nor severe emotional disturban ce.
Unfortunately, there remains an indication that many of our Brethren are
unaware of the admission criteria and application procedur es of the Covina
Home. Once again I would like to take this opportun ity to inform the Brethren
of the great aim we have in view.
To relieve the distress is a duty incumbent upon all men, but particularly
on Masons. Your Masonic Home seeks to relieve the distress of a worthy
Brother, his wife, widow and orphan. Most of the children we serve are the
grandchildren, nieces and nephews, and other minor ne.xt-of-kin of distressed
worthy Brother Master Masons or their widows. In this era, that distress is found
in the Mason or his widow who must assume responsibility for these children in
view of problems within the children's family. Most often today this is ongoing
domestic stress.
History shows the population of children in our Masonic Home in Covina
is r.elated to the complex social issues surround ing need, and also to the accuracy
of information about this Home by Masons in this jurisdiction.
POPULA TION
At fiscal year end we had served fifty-two (52) children. Four reached
maturity and pursued their independ ent living goals. On occasion our service
program is ei~her no longer .n~.eded by the family or the child, or needs escalate
beyond our license and ability to serve. This year twelve (12) children were
reunited with their families. One (1) child is on a leave of absence for an interim period.
Our youngest child is six years of age. Our oldest is eighteen years old having
just graduate d from high school.
~ix (6) children are elementa ry (K-5th grade) students. Ten (10) are intermediate students (6th-8th grades). Twenty (20) are high school (9th-12th

115

g!ades) of which two have recently graduate d. Thus we proudly serve thirty-six
(36) children at fiscal year end.
The Masonic Home children attend the public school system in Charter
Oak Unified School District which serves portions of the communities in
Covina San Dimas, and Glendora . Your Administ rator is a member of the
governing board of this Unified School District.
Through the generosity and love of our Brethren and their families, the following children have been served during this past fiscal year. Rememb er that
each name represent s a generatio n to follow and therefore you assure the
development of not only the one but, like parents, you are able to favorably touch
the future.
Again, the population of both our Masonic Homes is related to two basic
criteria; (1) need, and (2) the accura~yof informati on about this Home. It would
be most sad to be needed and yet fail to serve. Your Trustees have been altef!tive to this issue of information so to keep our Brethren informed about this
great charity -- The Masonic Homes of California.

CONCLUSION

REPORT OF CONTRIBUTIONS TO ENDOWMENT FUND

Our sincere and greatful thank you to Grand Master Leo B. Mark and to
the Grand Lodge Officers and Committeemen, all of whom have been
most supportive of the Endowment Program . We also wish to thank the
Masters, Wardens and Secretaries of the Lodges for their efforts in furthering this worthy program.
We extend a special thank you to the 77 ,810 Brothers who, through their
generosity, contributed $1,428,229 .43 to the Endowment Fund during the
past year.
.
We appreciate the splendid assistance and support we have received from
the Homes Board of Trustees, the Grand Secretary's office under the leadership of Grand Secretary Robert A. Klinger, assisted by Assistant Grand
Secretary H. Francis Lewis, and the hard working staff in the Grand Lodge
office.
My personal thank you to the members of the Endowment Board for
their dedicated efforts and the support extended to me over the past four
years .
Respectfully submitted,
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
ERNEST A. POOLEON, Chairman

COMMITTEE ON RECOGNITION OF
FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Due to the importance of available time, this Committee will only report on those
items requiring immediate attention.

Proposed Grand Lodge of Lebanon: During the past summer we received information that the Grand Orient of Italy was creating a Grand Lodge for Lebanon, this
did not happen; because in order to organize a Grand Lodge (Regular) there must be
at least three Regular operating Lodges in the territory and the only .Lodges operating
in Lebanon are under the jurisdiction ofth.e Grand Lodge of New York, and the latest
information we have &om New York is that these Lodges are not operating or if so,
under very difficult conditions.
Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile: This Grand Lodge, organized in New York and
operating in Boston, Massachusetts, was declared "irregular" by action of this Grand
Lodge in 1984, but as an act of aid and assistance to those Brethren, who were "members
in Good Standing" in Lodges in Iran prior to the Revolution of 1979, the Grand
Secretary was authorized to contin.ue issuing letters verifying that membershup in lieu
of a Dim.it, for purposes of Affiliation only.
Now the "irregular" Grand Lodge of Iran has established several Lodges with the
same names and numbers as those destroyed in Iran and conferred Degrees in this
Country, and do business from a Los Angeles address. In view of this, it is recommended that the Grand Secretary be relieved of the responsibility of verification of
membership in Iran in lieu of a Dimit. And, that anyone wishing to join a California
Lodge be required to file an Application for Degrees and pay all fees.
Fraternalization: It is well known that some Masons, members in California, lend
aid and comfort, communicate with and even visit the activities of the above "irregular"
Grand Lodge and it is recommended that they be dealt with in accordance with the
laws of our Grand Lodge.

71ie Committee on Jurisprodence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Grand Master Levitt's Recommendation No. 3 has been referred, reports as follows:
Grand Master Levitt recommended that the appointment of Senior and Junior
Wardens on Standing Committees should be optional with the Grand Master and not
mandatory.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as proposed in 1987 and as distributed
by the Grand Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent
of Grand Master Levitt.
Since this Recommendation, at the last Annual Communication, received less than
the five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it has been
carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication and a two-thirds
affirmative vote is now required for adoption. As a carry-over Recommendation, no
farther motion for adoption is necessary.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Our procedure now requires the appointment of one Senior Warden and one
Junior Warden to Standing Committees of more than five (5) members. Grand Master
Levitt wished to make it optional with the Grand Master.

Among the good things to be said for the appointment of Wardens as Committee
members are these:
1. They contribute new ideas.
2. They contribute the thinking of those less exposed to Grand Lodge.
3. They take back to their Lodges new insight and experience.
Grand Master Levitt recited the things which sometimes make it difficult to
appoint Wardens:
1. Many Wardens express the desire not to serve as they are too busy with their
duties to the Lodge.

2. It is impractical and, perhaps, harmful to the Craft to appoint some Senior
Wardens in October, because they then become Masters within the next several
months and are either unwilling to serve in both capacities or at least a substantial
burden is placed upon them.
Actually, the first suggestion these appointments should be made optional came
from the Special Study Commission on Grand Lodge Committee Structure. That
Commission reasoned that:
1. The first obligation of the Wardens is to attend and represent their Lodges on
the floor of Grand Lodge, and
2. To place a Warden on a working Committee would take him away from that
duty.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Last year the Policy and General Purposes Committee ~ecomm~nd.ed a "No" vote
on this Recommendation. However, we have had a change in our thinkmg.

that changes can be made and at the same time preserve the integrity of our image, as
well as respond to the concerns raised by some of you.

It may be that the merits of the old way seem less important in the face of the
reasons for a change and the practical difficulties Grand Masters face in making such
appointments. Additionally, the reasons cited for adhering to the old requirement are
perceived to be largely accruing to the individual Lodges. It appeared last year at least
a majority of the members of Grand Lodge did not agree.

At the 1987 Annual Communication, in determining as to whether proposed
legislation was consistent with the policies and general purposes of the Grand Lodge,
we looked first to history for guidance in considering the subject of alcoholic beverages
in meeting places and the related activities therein. It was the concensus of the
Committee, however, that on some occasions the general purposes of the Grand Lodge
can best be served by change. We believed then, as we do now, that it is time for reform
on this issue.

146

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The approval of this Recommendation does not preclude Grand Masters from
making such appointments, and we encourage them to continue the practice whenever
and wherever possible.

Some of the areas of reform apparent to us are:
- gr~at~r flexibility in determining suitable meeting places for prerequisite orgaruzat1ons;
- the right to rent or lease land or buildings owned by Masonic Lodges or Temple
Associations, for events or activities where alcoholic beverages are served, sold or
consumed, with certain checks and balances;
- the retention of restrictions that would preserve the dignity, integrity and sanctity
of the Lodge and the Lodge room.

Recommendation APPROVED.

MEETING PLACE OF MASONIC LODGES
AND PREREQUISITE ORGANIZATIONS
TI1e Committee 011 Jurisprodence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Grand Master Levitt's Recommendation No. 4 has been referred, reports as follows:

One of the duties of this Committee is to carefully and thoughtfully examine the
several matters assigned to it, and then report to you what we believe to be the best
policy to serve the general purposes of the Craft. It is our determination that, of the
several proposals concerning alcoholic beverages in meeting places, Resolution No.
87-23 and Resolution No. 88-19 will, if either is adopted, best serve those general
purposes and meet the policy concerns of the day. We will, accordingly, actively
support those Resoluti~ns in tum as they appear on the agenda.

Grand Master Levitt recommended that Masonic Lodges and prerequisite organizations be allowed to meet in buildings where alcoholic beverages are served,
provided there are separate entrances into the Lodge p~emises and into t~e area where
alcohol is, or may be, served and that annual and semi-annual Conventions or Communications be allowed to be held in buildings where alcoholic beverages are, or may
be served provided there is no adequate alternative facility available where alcoholic
be~erages are not served, and provided no alcohol is consumed in the meeting room.

As we did in 1987, we have reviewed Grand Master Levitt's Recommendation No.
4 and find it to contain several points of merit. It does not, however, in our opinion,
respond to the most critical areas of concern.

Your Committee finds that the legislation as proposed in 1987 and as distributed
by the Grand Secretary to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent
of Grand Master Levitt.

One of the rules of order, applicable to this Session, is that where two or more
issues of a similar nature, yet with areas of conflict, receive the required number of
votes for passage, the proposal with the greatest number of affirmative votes shall
prevail. For this reason we recommend a "No" vote on carry-over Recommendation
No.4.

Since this Recommendation, at the last Annual Communication, received less than
the five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it has been
carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication and two-thirds affirmative vote is now required for adoption. As a carry-over Recommendation, no further
motion for adoption is necessary.

The Committee on Temple Properties:
The Committee on Temple Properties heartily agrees with the amendments to
Section 2048 as proposed by Grand Master Levitt in his message to the Grand Lodge
last October.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

In reporting on the Special Committee Report of our Liquor Laws carried over

The Commitee 011 Youth Orders:

W~ expresse.d a dee~ appreciation for the time and effort spent by the Special
Committee. The rnformahon gleaned from other Jurisdictions was most informative.

Carry-over Grand Master's Recommendation No. 4 will, we feel, have no effect
on the day-to-day operation or the well-being of our Masonic Youth Groups.
Some Youth Groups find it necessary to meet in a room in a building in which
there may elsewhere be a bar. Also, some Youth Groups find it necessary to hold their
Annual Convention in a Hotel or Convention Center which also contains a bar.
All young people today, every day, in their schools from about the fourth grade
on, are exposed to and have easy access to a wide variety of chemical substances,
including alcoholic beverages. They also seem to have ample money to buy. We Masons
just cannot seem to change that scenario by passing resolutions here. Our continuing,
however, to set good, strong examples of character, respectability and good citizenship
in our communities will pay off. Our young people will notice, will approve and they
will emulate us.
The Youth Orders Committee sees no conflict or compromise here with respect
to our Masonic young people and therefore recommends that you vote in favor of
approving carry-over Grand Master's Recommendation No. 4.

be members of Grand Lodge. Members of this Grand Lodge are Past Masters of
constituent Lodges and therefore probably would have been exposed to questions
concerning alcoholic beverages during the conduct of their Masonic careers. This prior
experience assures opinions from men who would be most knowledgeable and com passionate in determining any recommendatio ns for the future. Those members
queried were asked to contact members of their own and nearby Lodges and to report
the consensus of opinion in respect to modification and clarification of California
Masonic Law as pertains to alcoholic beverages. It was estimated that approximately
2,800 Masons were contacted and had their opinions reported. Most of the opinions
were from Lodge Officers, Officers' Associations, Masters, Wardens, and members
active in Lodge.
When the questionnaires were tabulated, 40% of the respondents desired no
change in our law, but that left (i()% desiring some modification. Most respondents,
including the (i()% recommending some change or liberalization, felt that modifying
the law would do nothing to increase Lodge attendance nor applications for membership and cited similar membership problems in other Fraternal organizations such as
the Elks Clubs.
However, those favoring some change did so, for the most part, for economic
reasons. Those favoring change generally agreed that Masonic organizations sho uld
be able to rent their facilities, under proper and equitable rules, for non-Masonic
purposes, such as wedding receptions. Grand Master's Recommendati on No. 4 from
1987 and Carry-over Resolution No. 87-23 do not address this question.
Many of the responses suggested that a Lodge should not be displaced from its
meeting place merely because a restaurant or some other beverage-servin g organization occupied quarters in the same building and so your Study Committee made
provision to accomodat~ that recommendatio n. Also, it was agreed that those Masonically affiliated organizations which had no meeting place of their own should not be
prohibited from renting space for certain periodic meetings in a facility where alcoholic
beverages are served.

It should be noted and emphasized that, to the best of our knowledge, no such
in-depth study has been made by the proponents of other proposed legislation concerning alcoholic beverages. It is improbable that equitable legislation might be
proposed without having sought the general opinion of the many members of this
Grand Lodge.
The fourth element is found in the one word - EQUITY. This word is the very
foundation of most laws, rules and regulations, whether it be in sports competition
(such as the recent Olympic Games or in the rules of golf) or in the application of law
in our system of justice.
To be equitable means to be fair and just. For example, Masonic Law as well as
Masonic tradition, since the proverbial time immemorial, has held that a Mason should
not be permitted to do in one Masonic organization that which he is prohibited from
doing in another Masonic organization. Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson stated
this premise very well when he declared in 1957 that "it would be IPOSt unfair to the
Blue Lodges if their members could band together in another body and endeavor to
do what the Lodges cannot do". Section 2612 of our California Masonic Code
elaborates further, "All members of organizations within the territorial jurisdiction of
this Grand Lodge, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master

PROCEED INGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

Mason, shall be subject to the same standards of conduct and propriety as are or may
be imposed upon Master Masons in this jurisdiction". Your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes has espoused this philosophy of equity on numersous occasions in
response to various proposals dealing with many different subjects. Even so, there
appear to be some proposed changes to our law to be decided at this Communic ation
which would virtually eliminate any alcohol restriction s in affiliated or concordan t
bodies. One sure way to disturb peace and harmony in Lodges is to be inequitabl e in
the application of Masonic Law to all Masons in the jurisdictio n of this Grand Lodge.
It is grossly unjust and unfair to grant privileges to some Master Masons while not
granting the same privileges to all. ff you should approve Resolution 88-19, all control
over prerequisi te organizatio ns will be removed, thus deleting equality of treatment to
all Masons.
