Th Committee on Taxation:
Carry-over Resolution 87-23 and Resolutions 88-19, 88-21 and 88-33 have been
referred to your Committee on Txation to comment on the possible tax consequences
of each of them. To understand the possible tax consequences, it is important to
understand how Masonic Lodges and Masomc Temple Associations are taxed.

Masonic Lodges are exempt from a Federal and California income taxes, regardless of the amount of income from dues, interest, dividends or income from other
investments, with certain exceptions. A Lodge is taxable on income from a trade or
business which is unrelated to the fraternal purposes of the Lodge. When exempt
organizations, such as Masonic Lodges, compete with taxpaying businesses, the income
from that competitive activity is taxed to remove any economic advantage which exempt
status might have conferred. This income is known as "urelated business income". For
example, net income from a working oil interest would be taxable because such an
interest is considered a trade or business.
To constitute a trade or busmcss, however, the activity must be re.gularly carried
on. This does not include periodic events. Operating a restaurant constitutes a trade
or business. Holding periodic dinners does not constitute a trade o~ bu.siness. In
addition, income from events conducted by tax-exempt fraternal orgamzat1ons, such
as Masonic Lodges, are not taxable if substantially all of the labor required to hold the
event is performed by the Lodge without compensation.
There are also potential California Sales and use tax consequences to certain
Lodge events. A sales tax is assessed upon the sale of tangible personal property. The
sale of tangible personal property includes furnishin~ meals a~ well as suppl~ng
merchandise at garage sales or bazaars for a purchase pnce, even 1f the purchase pnce
is labeled a "donation".
There is one exception to the Sales and use tax available to Lodges, however. Social
clubs and fraternal organizations, such as Masonic Ldges, are not subject to the sales
tax on their receipts from furnishing meals if the meals are furnished exclusively to

requirements

Any other transfers of tangible personal property by the Lodge, such as at garage
sales or bazaars, are subject to the sales tax. If the Lodge is subject to the sales tax, it
must apply for a California Seller's permit. These can be obtained from the local office
of the State Board of Equalizaiton.
These unrelated business income tax and sales and use tax rules apply to Masonic
Temple Associations also.
The adoption of Resolution 87-23 would permit Masonic Lodges and Temple
Associations to serve alcoholic beverages. For the reasons discussed above, serving
alcoholic beverages could result in income tax liability unless alcoholic beverages are
never sold but given away, are sold infrequently or are only sold at events where
substantially all the labor required to hold the event is performed without compensation. The sale of alcoholic beverages would likely be subject to sales tax.

the restriction which has been in effect since September 27, 1957 against the formation

a subsequent Annual Communication its proposed constitution and by-laws.

MASONIC LODGE SCHOLARSHIP AWARDS
(87-33)
The Committee on Jurisprodence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 87-33 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to authorize the expenditure of Lodge
funds for individual scholarship awards.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponents.
Since this Resolution, at the last Annual Communication, received less than the
five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it has been
carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication and a two-thirds
affirmative vote is now required for adoption. As a carry-over Resolution, no further
motion for adoption is necessary.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
At present, our Masonic Law limits the expenditure of Lodge funds for scholarship
purposes to nominal amounts awarded in programs related to Public Schools Week.
Adoption of Resolution No. 87-33 would eliminate this prohibition and permit each
Lodge to decide for itself whether to sponsor a scholarship program, to the extent that
the Lodge could afford such a program. Adoption of this Resolution would not require
Lodges to have scholarship programs. A Lodge could weigh the benefits against the
costs of a scholarship program. It would be left to the discretion of the Brethren in the
Lodge whether to undertake a scholarship program. If undertaken by a Lodge, we
believe that such a program might increase our members appreciation for education
and certainly would increase the regard for Masonry by every citizen supporting
accessible education for all. We believe that such benefits are consistent with the
policies of this Grand Lodge.

A quarterly dues payment structure represents a burden to our Secretaries as
Section 2814a states that "the Secretary should send statements as least quart~rly to
those whose dues are not paid quarterly in advance", and most Brethren pay their dues
on a per annum basis.

The Policy and General Purposes Committee therefore, recommends a "Yes" vote
on Resolution No. 87-33.

Further, Section 2816 of the Code provides for cases of special ~n~ideration
wherein it states• ... unless for special reasons shown, the Lodge shall remit his dues or
grant him further time for payment".

The argumen t relative to the right of a candidat e to select the Holy Writings of his
choice on which to be obligated has been before this Grand Lodge on numerou s
occasions in the past. Your Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes consistently
opposed this change in Grand Lodge policy, citing studies which contend that the use
of the Holy Bible in our Degrees does not in any way imply that Freemaso nry is limited
to a Christian belief.
Last year the Committ ee reversed its position, stating in part, as follows:
"Masonry does not require a man to have or believe in a particula r religion.
Masonry only requires that a man believe in a Supreme Being, a deity which may be
known by different names, dependin g on what part of the world and what customs,
culture or religion is involved.
As Masonry makes no distinctio n between race, creed, or religion, and requires
only that a candidate for the Degrees of Freemaso nry believe in God and come well
recomme nded under the tongue of good report, the candidat e should be allowed to
select the Holy Writings of bis choice upon which to be obligated and those writings

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

should be those which he most reveres, believes and res~cts, in order t? m~st impress
upon him the importance of the Degree and the solemnity of the occasion.

It was the recommendation of that Committee that the Holy Bible continue to be
the only book upon which all candidates are obligated, bearing fully in mind that the
use of the Holy Bible in our Degrees does not in any way imply that Freemasonry is
J.jroited to a Christian belief. The findings of that Committee as reported here in 1977

we must urge a "No" vote.

important of these considerations, however, is the great number of changes m our ~aw
and ritual and additional problems for Lodges which would result from the substitu-·
tion of a~other book for the Holy Bible. For example, if a man claimed t~at he
considered the dictionary to be his Holy Writings, the Lodge would have no choice but
to accede to his wish and obligate him upon that book.
Because of the complex nature of the study, the Committee deemed it advisable
and necessary to seek additional advice of those more expert in the field of Theology
and Holy Writings. Opinions were therefore solicited f~om Brothers l_loland A. ~a.ch
and Rabbi Edgar Magnin, both former Grand Chaplams and recognized authonlles
in the field of Theology.
"Both of these former Grand Chaplains stated that in their opinion, the practice
of substituting other books for the Holy Bible in obligating a candi~ate could le~d to
a myriad of problems. Both advised against instituting such. a prachce ..To substitu~e
another book for the Holy Bible in our Degrees would requ1Te substantive changes m
our law to permit the necessary revisions to t?e adopted C~ifornia ritual. A change
such as this could well lead to further, undesirable changes m our p~esent syste~ of
ritual. The problems which would be encountered would far outweigh any possible
advantage to the Craft or to any individual."

Your Committee on Ritual respectfully recommends a "No" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

CHARITY COMMITIEE TO REMIT DUES

(87-46)
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution 87-46 has been referred,
reports as follows:
The proponents of this R esolution seek to change the procedure for the remission
of dues so as to permit the Charity Committee of the Lodge to recommend the
remission without stating the names of the members involved.
Your Committee fmds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponents.
Since this Resolution, at the last Annual Communication, received less than the
five-sixths vote required for adoption, but did receive a majority vote, it bas been
carried over for reconsideration at this Annual Communication and a two-thirds
affirmative vote is now required for adoption. As a carry-over Resolution, no further
motion for adoption is necessary.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the procedure for the remission
of dues so as to permit the Charity Committee of the Lodge to r ecommend the
remission without stating the name(s) of the member(s) involved.
Action by the Grand Master of the Lodge in accordance with Section 20860 of the
California Masonic Code will shelter the affected member from the embarrassment of
having his name placed before the Lodge.
On occasions a needy Brother has allowed himself to be suspended for non-payment of dues rather than expose himself to such embarrassment.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee concurs with the proponents of this
Resolution and recommends a "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe and gave it to his neighbor; and
this was testimony in Israel". That is why they wear the Golden Slipper. It was designed
to be a lady's slipper of gold, it being of gold to express one of the finest gifts that can

Our Masonic name and insignia, including the Square and Compass are registered
with the California Secretary of State. A court ruling against an abuser, permanent ly
enjoined the use of the words "Mason" or "Masonic" or the Square and Compass
emblem.
In 1955, Grand Master Clausen ruled, ~e unauthoriz ed wearing of fraternal
organization insignia is prohibited by Penal Code Section 538(b ). A ladies' branch of
a Grotto of the Mystic Order Veiled Prophets may not wear an emblem or pin which
includes Masonic insignia such as a Square and Compass". California Masonic Code

which entitles them to use this Masonic emblem and asks the Grand Lodge to correct

In 1986 Grand Lodge approved Grand Master Driskell's Decision No. 3 which

As a former Grand Lodge Inspector it has always been the custom to excuse any
of our Jewish Brothers from attending any Grand Lodge function whenever in that
member's judgment be found that his attendance would conflict with his religious
beliefs.
To recognire any minority group by adopting a special interest Resolution would
only open pandora's box and could create a ripple effect by inviting other minority
groups to seek similar recognition by the Resolutions media.
For example, our Italian members could take exception to holding our Annual
Communications on Columbus Day, which has been our custom for many years and
which we will be doing tomorrow. Or our Chinese members could take objection to
holding our Annual Communication on the Anniversary date of the founding of the
National Republic of China. Also, there are undoubtly many other dates or occasions
among special interest groups which we are not aware of.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 88-11 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to obtain for each Inspector an individual
\'Ole in the Grand Lodge.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponents.

This Resolution seeks to amend the Constitution and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The adoption of this Resolution would give each Masonic Inspector a separate
vote in the Grand Lodge, in addition to the vote which each Inspector now shares with
the other Past Masters of his Lodge.
There is no question that our Inspectors arc experienced and talented and add
much to the work of this Grand Lodge. As a Past Master, each Inspector now bas the
right to address this Grand Lodge during its deliberations and to propose legislation
for its consideration. But, your Committee does not think it appropriate to give each
Inspector a separate vote. Grand Lodge is not a collection of Lodge Line Officers and
Past Masters but an assembly of Masonic Lodges. Each Lodge bas an equal voice in
Grand Lodge, regardless of how large or small the Lodge may be. Thus, each Lodge

long standing policy and practice of the Craft which we should not abandon by gi\/Ulg
each Inspector a separate vote.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee therefore, recommends a "No" vote
on Resolution No. 88-11.

and the Grand Lecturer which shall meet monthly, at the call of the Grand Master, and
shall be chaired by him. The function of the Executive Committee shall be to counsel
with the Grand Master concerning the operation and affairs of the Grand Lodge, and
to ·perform such other duties as shall be designated by the Grand Master."
Respectfully submitted,
Gary D. Miller, PM No. 576
Leroy Chambers, PM No. 576
Robert E. Winterton, Sr., M No. 576

The Committee on Finance:
It is the opinion of the Grand Lodge Finance Committee that should the Resolution No. 14 pass, that there will be no significant impact on the expenses of Grand
Lodge, assuming the Executive Committee meets when the Officers are together on
Grand Lodge functions.

Therefore we do not make a recommendation on the Resolution. .

DUTIES OF ASSISTANT GRAND TREASUR ER
(88-15)

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and
Finance.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 88-14 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to expand the Executive Committee to
include the Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponents.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Constitution and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

185

The proponents of this Resolution seek to add to the duties of the Assistant Grand
Treasurer and to provide for him to act in the absence or inability of the Grand
Treasurer.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WI;IEREAS, the California Masonic Code, Section 1112 specifically provides for
:~Assistant Grand Secretary to act for the Grand Secretary in his absence or inability;

~EREAS, the California Masonic Code, Section 1104 does not so provide for
the AssJStant Grand Treasurer to act for the Grand Treasurer in his absence or
inability; and
WHEREAS , Section 1022 of the California Masonic Code does authorize the
Grand Master to fill a vacancy occurring in any elective office of the Grand Lodge but
'
..inability lo act" is not defined as creating a vacancy.

The Grand Master, between Grand Lodge Annual Communications, possesses all
the executive powers of the Grand Lodge.

NOW, THEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 1104 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

Before 1981, it was a common practice for the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand
Master and the Grand Wardens to discuss the operation and affairs of the Grand
Lodge, but the practice depended on the desire of the Grand Master. Some consulted;
some did not.

. "The Grand Treasurer may, with the approval of the Grand Master, appoint an
Assistant Grand Treasurer, for whose official acts he shall be responsible and who
shall be considered an appointive officer of the Grand Lodge and who shali assist the
Grand Treasu'!r in the discharge of his duties and shall perform such other duties as
may be prescnbed by the Grand Treasurer and, in his absence or inability, shall actfior

In 1981, this Grand Lodge formally recognized those officers as ~he ~ecuti~
Committee of this Grand Lodge. Those officers represent the progressive line. Their
formal consultation was believed to assure greater continuity in the adminis~ation of
Grand Lodge affairs. This should not be confusing. The Grand Master is t~e executive.
He simply has the formal advice of those who, in succeeding years, will be Grand
Masters. That achieves the purpose which was desired. But make no mistake, the
Grand Master may ignore the advice.

The Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary and the Grand Lecturer perform
important duties, but in those offices they do not progress to the office of Grand
Master. Their consultation is available when required.
There is no need to expand the Executive Committee.

~. ·

Respectfully submitted,
Ralph H. Head, PM No. 352

Robert A. Klinger, PM No. 120

TENURE OF SERVICE
COMMITTEES, BOARDS, INSPECTORS
(88-17)
The proponent oC this Resolution seeks to limit consecutive service on one
Committee, Board or other entity, or as an Inspector, to a total of nine years, including

years served as Committee Chairman and to limit the tenure of Committee Chairmen
to no more than 5 years.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, some balance must be struck between experience and inexperience,
bctwccn old ideas and new ideas, between the desire to honor those who have served
the Grand Lodge by continuing service and the need to allow more people to serve the
Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the problem has been faced in some cases by legislation. The
California Masonic Code allows ten years as the maximum tenure for Committee
Chairman (CMC 1201); and
WHEREAS, there is an infonnal understanding that Inspectors shall serve at least

five but no more than ten years; and

WHEREAS, all Boards of Trustees are limited to three consecutive, three year
terms of service. A Trustee may be reappointed but only after the lapse of one year

(CMC 1302).
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 1116 of the California
Masonic Code be amended by adding after the first paragraph, the following para-

graph:

closer than anything that has preceded it.

SELLING FOOD AND NON-ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES
AT COMMUNITY EVENTS
(88-21)

Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponents.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit Lodges to sell food and non-alcoholic beverages at local community events to raise funds for general Lodge use.

This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
WHEREAS, many communities throughout the state and particularly the small
ones, celebrate by having an annual community eve.nt such as a fair, picnic, parade,
etc. to celebrate pride in their community and the country. At these events, most
community organizations participate. It is time for Masonry to be recognized by the
community. Also, the income generated from a food booth would help the small Lodges
by providing additional funds for repair and maintenance of the building (which is
becoming increasingly more expensive), as well as making it possible to have Lodge
activities at a more nominal charge or on a minimal basis. This would not only be
beneficial to the older members, many of whom are on a fixed retirement income, but
to all its members; and

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

WHEREAS, it is a fact of reality, that it is virtually impossible for small Lodges to
exist on their dues alone, even at double the present rate.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2070 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"A Lodge shall not sponsor, or by resolution or otherwise sanction, or permit the
use of the name of the Lodge in connection with, or for the purpose of furthering any
collateral financial undertaking, or commercial venture, whether for profit or not,
which shall not have been approved by the Grand Master, nor shall any member of any
Lodge be permitted to do so except in his individual capacity, and without the use of
the name of the Lodge; provided, however, that notwithstanding the prohibition hereinbefo~ set forth, a Lodge may participate in local community fairs, celebrations, and

!

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that Lodges and organizations
subject to its jurisdiction should not engage in any commercial ventures. Among the
reasons in support of this policy are concerns that such ventures might reflect on the
dignity of this organization and that questionable business practices might give the
general public an unfavorable opinion of Freemasonry. There have also been some
difficulties in trying to control the commercial activities of a few organizations under
the existing restrictive regulations.

The proponents of this Resolution argue that many Lodges are experiencing
severe financial problems which their present dues structure cannot overcome. They
believe this change will offer another source of funds to supplement their dues income.
They also make the point that this would provide an incentive for our Lodges to become
more involved in local activities, thereby achieving greater community recognition.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes that approval of this
Resolution will mark a distinct change in Grand Lodge policy. However, after careful
consideration, the Committee believes that the potential financial benefits to the
constituent Lodges and the greater participation in community activities make this
change in policy a proper one.
We therefore, recommend a "Yes" vote.

WHEREAS, Section 2316 states, in part, that Lodge funds, whether derived from
fees, dues, rental, profit or otherwise, are trust funds set apart for the payment of the
necessary expenses of the Lodge and for the special calls for charity for which it was
instituted; and the Lodge shall not use or permit the use of its funds or property or any
part of them for any other thing whatwev~r except, as thereinafter in our Code
permitted; and

WHEREAS, Section 2320 does provide for discretionary expenditures for payment to Lodge Officers attending Annual Communications, testimonials for a retiring
Master, floral pieces for an ill or deceased Brother or family, compensation for an
Organist, contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund or to the California
Masonic Foundation in lieu of flowers for an ill or deceased Brother, and purchase of
trowel for presentation to a newly raised Master Mason; and
WHEREAS, Section 2904b restricts a Masonic Service Bureau from donating any
of its funds to the Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes; and
WHEREAS, Lodges and Masonic Service Bureaus, as a matter of tradition, have
presented to Grand Masters, in token of appreciation and esteem for their attendance
at Lodge and Bureau sponsored Grand Lodge ceremonies, receptions and visitations,
contributions, in their name, to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, California
Masonic Foundation and other Masonic related charities; and
WHEREAS, our California Masonic Code does not permit this type of expenditure of Lodge funds.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2320 of the California
Masonic Code be amended by adding at the end thereof, the following paragraph:

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 88-23 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution seelcs to authorize contributions from Lodge or
Masonic Service Bureau funds to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, California

his designee.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponent of this Resolution see.ks to authorize Lodges and Masonic Service
Bureaus to contribute a nominal donation to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund,
California Masonic Foundation, or Masonic Youth Groups in honor of the Grand
Master.
Despite regulations to the contrary, Lodges and Masonic Service Bureaus have in
the past made nominal donations to our Masonic Charity funds, foundations, and our
Youth organizations on behalf of, or in honor of the Grand Master in token of
appreciation and esteem for his services to the Craft. This is in keeping with our
obligation to render charitable support to the needy, and particularly to ow Brothers
and their families.
The California Masonic Code Section 2320 does provide for a donation to the
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund or to the California Masonic Foundation in lieu of
flowers for an ill or deceased Brother. This Committee feels that a contribution made
on behalf of, or in honor of the Grand Master would be equally fitting in fulfilling at
least a part of our charitable obligations.
Therefore, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.

REINSTATEMENT OF MULTIPLE MEMBERS
(88-24)

shall forthwith suspend his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction but shall be

The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic Code
to provide that restoration of a member who has been suspended for non-payment of
dues, automatically reinstates him in other Lodges in which said member also held
membership.

To the Most Worshipful Grund Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Subsection 6 of Section 2402 of the California Masonic Code appears
to be very unclear in that it provides that in cases of a member suspended for
non-payment of dues, "reinstatement by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of California...shall immediately and automatically restore (a member), to membership
in every other Lodge in this Jurisdiction of which he was a member upon payment of
any dues required, or the performance of any other obligation required for such
restoration to membership".; and
WHEREAS, the said Section does not say that there is any obligation on the part
of the member to make application for restoration to the other Lodge or Lodges
although the Grand Secretary's office is interpreting it so - even to the extent of not
allowing the member to attend the Lodge in which he was just restored until be makes
application to and is restored in the other Lodge or Lodges; and
WHEREAS, this interpretation seems to violate every principle of brotherly love
and affection as professed by our Fraternity, because the only possible reason that
Grand Lodge should require such additional payment would be so the other Lodges
could extort some back dues from the reinstated Brother.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Subsection 6 of Section 2402 of
the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Suspension by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of th.is Grand Lodge for non-payment
of dues of a multiple member shall immediately, and of itself, suspend his membership
in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, and the Secretary of any Lodge suspending such a
member shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which the multiple member holds membership. Lilce notice shall be given in case of
reinstatement by a Lodge in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California which
shall immediately and automatically restore him to membership in every other Lodge
in this Jurisdiction of which he was a member."
"When non-payment of dues is the cause of suspension, such action shall become
effective only after a sixty-day prior Notice of Intent to Suspend has been sent to every
other Lodge in which the member holds membership, during which period such other
Lodge may contact the member in an effort to avoid such suspension. If within said
sixty-day period such member has failed to obtain good standing in all Lodges involved,
be shall be suspended, and such suspension shall immediately terminate his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction."

"Suspension by a Lodge in any other Grand Jurisdiction for non-payment of dues
bandied in the same manner as provided in this section for members suspended by a
Lodge in this Jurisdiction by giving sixty days notice, and provided further, that the
restoration of such a member shall be in the same manner as provided in this Code."

Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend Subsection 6 of Section 2402 of
the California Masonic Code entitled, "Multiple Membership", so as to provide that
restoration of a Brother to Good Standing, who previously had been suspended for
non-payment of dues, automatically reinstates him in all other Lodges in which the
Brother also held membership, without first having to pay all dues owed to or to
complete any other obligation required for Restoration to Membership in the other
Lodge or Lodges of his Multiple Membership. The proponents would do this by
striking the words "upon payment of any dues required or the performance of any other
obligation required for such Restoration to Membership" from the last three lines of
the first paragraph of said Subsection 6.
When a member of a Masonic Lodge applies for and accepts Multiple Masonic
Membership where it is allowed, he agrees to pay dues to the other Masonic Lodges
and to abide by all of the rules and regulations of the other Masonic Jurisdiciton
involved. It is only reasonable, therefore, that the Brother see.king Restoration for
non-payment of dues in a Masonic Lodge should be required to pay any delinquent
dues owed to his other multiple Lodges before Restoration to Masonic Membership
is completed. If the member in question does not wish to pay dues to more than one

PROCEEDI NGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

Lodge, after bringing his dues current in all Lodges, be may then request a Dimit from
the multiple Lodge in which be no longer desires to be a member.

To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Policy and General Purposes Committee believes that Section 2402 of the
California Masonic Code should remain as presently written, and therefore, recommends a "No" vote on this Resolution.

Adoption of Resolution No. 88-26 would eliminate the requirement that Masters
and Wardens learn the proficiency in the Candidate's Lecture of the Third Degree
before installaiton in office. This requirement has been debated five times in the last
twenty-two years. Each time, this Committee has questioned the wisdom of this
requirement, for two reasons. First, we do not believe that learning more ritual results
in better leadership. Memorizing our work, while important to a love for understanding
of the Craft, does not sharpen a man's ability to lead. Second, the Third Degree
proficiency requirement may actually inhibit good men from accepting a Lodge Line

attendance on all Stated Meetings, Degree nights, or Officer's practices, Schools of
Instruction, and other Officer's meetings, with the resultant absence from family life
at home; and

assuming the first position to be that of Junior Steward, and advancing one station each
year; and

Officer's positions, in order that the Lodge can be able to function.

TM Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudenc e to which Resolution No. 88-27 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to allow a Past Master of this Jurisdiction
who has served as a Master or Warden not more than 3 years preceding his Installation,
to serve as a Master or Warden without examination as to his qualifications and
proficiency.
Your Committee finds that the legislation as distributed by the Grand Secretary
to the Constituent Lodges is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponent.
This Resolution seeks to amend the Ordinances and a five-sixths affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 88-27 proposes to allow a Past Master of this Jurisdiction who has
held the office of Master or Warden within the preceding three years, to be installed
as Master or Warden without examination as to his qualifications or proficiency.
It is true that many Lodges have difficulty in encouraging their members to attend
Lodge. It is true that some of the older members are reluctant to take on the duties of
being an Officer of the Lodge for a number of reasons. Many Officers are remiss in
their duty to attend meetings, practices, Officers Association meetings and Schools of
Instruction as required of those who make a commitment to hold office. Many Past
Masters are asked to again hold office in their Lodges. However, relieving a Past
Master of re-qualifying for the office of Warden or Master will not alleviate these
problems.

What is most important is that our Officers demonstrate their qualifications and
proficiency in fulfilling the duties of Warden and Master, and that the team of Officers
which exemplifies the Degrees, does so in the best possible manner.
If a Past Master has held the office of Warden or Master within the previous three
years, it shouJd take only a short time for him to review the ritual to again demonstrate
his proficiency, and to review the necessary material in order to re-qualify in his
knowledge of policy and procedures in discharging the duties of that office. The offices
of Warden and Master are extremely important to the success of the Lodge, and no
short-cuts should be taken in preparing one to assume such an important position.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
We can appreciate the intent of the proponent of this Resolution. Many Past
Masters have diligently maintained their ritualistic capability beyond their term of
office. They are to be commended for their efforts. We fear, though, that this is not
equally true of every Past Master.
We suggest that the Past Master who is so dedicated to our Craft to have kept his
ritual intact, wouJd be proud to demonstrate his continued proficiency, in any or all of
the three Degrees. He would not regard th~ requirement to do so to be unreasonably

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

burdensome or demeaning. Indeed, the Inspectors are required to demonstrate their
proficiency in all three Degrees on a yearly basis.

The Committee on Policy and Generol Purposes:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to amend the California Masonic Code to
provide additional methods for correcting a possible mistake on the ballot on an
applicant.

It would seem the present system of handling the balloting on an applicant has
been working well for many years and provides ample safeguards for the rights of the
applicant and the peace and harmony of the Lodge.
No amount of procedures and additional safeguards would absolutely guarantee
there would never be an abuse of the rights of an applicant. But there must be placed
in our procedures some practical limit to which we can go in seeking those safeguards.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels the present system is
adequate and recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Ritual:
The proponent of this Resolution correctly states that we should be balloting upon
only good men; that only men meeting our requirements would have been recommended by two members of our Lodge and have passed the investigation by three
others. He also states, equally correctly, that those balloting are also honest and
honorable men.
As we all know, upon finding a single black cube, the Master is obligated to reballot
to correct a possible mistake. Upon finding a single cube a second time, the Candidate
is rejected.

At this point, the proponent asks to either ballot a third time or to permit him to
appoint another Investigating Committee. If the second investigation is full and
favorable, and if the dissenting Brother has not made a formal objection (which be is
Wlt required to do), the Master will declare the first 1:6'.Q ballots in error and the
Candidate elected. To suggest this, the Master must believe one of two things. Either:
1. A mistake was made on the second ballot also, a situation difficult to accept, or
2. One of those balloting, one who has already passed the test of the ballot box, is
not honest or honorable in casting his ballot, thus attributing to him moral or
ethical standards inferior to those attributed to the applicant.

Lodges throughou t California have adopted the Life Membersh ip program as
authorized by Section 2804 of the Califorma Masonic Code. Section 2806 of the
California Masonic Code requires that the Lodge Secretary mail, first class, annually,
the new Life Membersh ip card to the last known address of the member. In the event
that the membersh ip card is returned by the Post Office, and after six consecutive years
of being "unclaimed" or "Address Unknown", the seventh year the Secretary sends the
card by registered mail to the last known address of the member. If returned, the fact
is reported to the Lodge at the Stated Meeting and made note thereof in the Lodge
minutes. The member's name is removed from the roll books and trasmitted to Grand
Lodge with his Annual Report that the Life Member has been removed from the rolls
and the reason therefor.
The yearly dues card helps to keep the members' addresses current and the Lodge
roster updated. If a permanen t card is wued a Lodge can easily lose contact with it's
members and be required to continue to pay their per capita tax to Grand Lodge.
Section 2806 of the California Masonic Cod.e provides a method for purging the
roster oflost members and thus avoiding the per capita tax.
The current Sections to the California Masonic Code are adequate and the better
arguments are against changing the current Life Membersh ip Certificate.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommen ds a "No" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to exempt fifty year members from paying
dues and Lodges from paying per capita sums for those members.
Resolutions similar to this have been presented in 1969, 1973, 1975, 1984and1986
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee recommended a "No" vote in each~
as the financial effect of this Resolution, if passed, would unnecessarily increase per
capita tax and thereby place an even heavier burden on the constituent Lodges.
Over six hundred Fifty-year pins were presented last year alone. While it is
impossible to determine the exact number of Fifty-year members still living today, over
35,000 pins have been presented to date.
Many Fifty and Seventy-five year members can afford to pay dues. For those who
.
can not, there is a procedure to relieve them of that duty.
We appreciate desires to reward a member for fifty years of faithful service, but
the financial impact of incorporating an automatic relief from paying dues far outweighs the benefits.
Therefore, your Policy and General Purposes Committee again urges a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
We are unable to determine the number of fifty-year Masons now and in the future
and the loss of per capita assessment on those Brothers.
Your Committee on Finance is unable to estimate an accurate financial impact
under this Resolution, but it could be considerable and in an effort to keep expenses
at a minimum, we recommend a "No" vote.

Resolution.

71le Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Once again we are asked to approve the playing of Bingo in our Masonic Temples
provided that it is authorized by a local ordinance and that all state and local laws ar~
com~~· All r~ipts, as d~fmed by state law, are to be divided equally between
the California Masoruc Foundat10n and the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund.
Whether or not we approve of the playing of Bingo in our Masonic Temples, and
whether or not, as proposed, it might raise money for two worthwhile charities there
are reasons to question whether our Lodges and other Masonic groups can sat~fy the
legal requirements for conducting such games.

=

~on 3~..5 of the Cali!ornia.Penal Code allows Bingo games to be conducted
onlym those. etties and counties which have adopted ordinances allowing Bingo to be
Section 326.5 also requires that Bingo games must be open to the general

~e some of the cities and counties in California have enacted ordinances

permitting the playing of Bingo, many have not. In those areas which have approved

223

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the playing of Bingo, there are strict and sometimes costly licensing requirem~nts. In
addition there are often limitations as to the number of licenses which can be 1SSued.

The adoption of Resolution 88-33 would permit Masonic Lodges and Temple
Associations to conduct bingo games for the benefit of the California Masonic Foundation and the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund. For the reasons discussed in our
report on Resolution 87-23, any profit earned could result in income tax liability unless
such events are held infrequently or substantially all the labor required to hold such
events is performed without compensation. It is irrelevant that the proceeds are given
to charity. The sale of tangible personal property at such bingo games could be subject
to sales tax.

222

Adoption of this Resolution would therefore, permit the playing of Bingo in only
a limited number of our Lodges. Since ordinances permitting the playing of Bingo vary
from one area to another and since any violation of the State laws constitutes a
misdemeanor, Lodges undertaking this activity would have to exercise extreme caution.
Guidance from Grand Lodge in this matter would not be possible because of the
different requirements in each community.
Finally my Brethren, we must ask ourselves if this is the kind of activity we want to
see in our Lodges. Where Bingo is permitted it is a legal gambling activity. In areas
where demand for licenses is great, we already hear about large games being organized
to drive out the smaller operators. Since the public attending these games has, for the
most part, no ties to the sponsoring organization, they will go where the action is and
where the prizes are larger.
Adoption ofthis Resolution would represent a significant change in Grand Lodge
policy. It would approve a form of legalized public gambling in our Lodges. Because
of the limitations imposed by State and Local laws it would extend this approval to a
limited n.u mber of Lodges in this Jurisdiction.

"MASONRY INTO MEN"

recognition that may have come my way, I would still say that the time that I
have spent in Masonry, and in Masonic related activities, is the best investment
of time that I could have possibly made. I have received from Freemasonry
much, much more that I have given to it. And those of you in this audience today,
who have sacrificed time and money to be in attendance at Grand Lodge, undoubtedly share those sentiments. If there are some of us who feel that we have
gotten so much out of Masonry, for whom it has been such a rewarding experience, why is it that our Fraternity is in trouble? Why do young men particularly no longer seem to be attracted to our Fraternity?

CHARLES H. ALEXANDER, GRAND ORATOR
Most Worshipful Grand Master, fellow Grand Lodge Officers, Visitors from other
Grand Jurisdictions, members of the Grand Lodge, Brethren all.
Whal an awesome responsibility, but whal a great and distinct privilege
it is to have lhe opportunity of addressing the Grand Lodge of California at this
Annual Communication. And what a great privilege it has been to represent this
Grand Lodge at various ceremonies and functions up and down this state during
this Grand Lodge year. I want to express my grateful and sincere appreciation
to Most Worshipful Grand Master Leo B. Mark for this appointment and this
opportunity to serve your Grand Lodge, and I am sure that in doing so, I speak
not only for myself, but for the other appointive Grand Lodge Officers as well.
They, other than the Grand Chaplain, do not have the opportunity of speaking
to you. It has been a great and rewarding experience for all of us who comprise
your Grand Lodge Officers of 1988.
It is now almost forty years since I was raised to the sublime degree of
Master Mason. As I look back on that moment, a young man not yet twenty-two
years of age, little did I dream that I would ever be in attendance at Grand
Lodge, let alone have the opportunity to address you. But, my brethren, I foe!
that I am here today primarily because of the fact that when I took my degrees,
although I was still a very young man, there were some good brothers who took
the time to extend to me, both literally and symbolically, the hand of brotherly
love, and truly made me feel a part of this great fraternity. Bul like most young
men my immediate priorities did not allow for much participation in Masonry,
except for occasional attendance at degrees and stated meetings. I got married,
entered my chosen profession of teaching, and began a family. But let me go
back to that first teachingjob. I was located about a six hour drive from my ho me
Lodge, so ther e was little opportunity for me to have Masonic fellowship in my
own Lodge. In that to wn, it was the custom to invite lhe newly hired teachers to
be the guests of the R otary Club as one way of introducing them to the community. Several members of the Rotary, who also happened to be Masons,
noticed my Masonic ring, and invited me to attend their Lodge at my earliest
opportunity. What a warm feeling it gave me, and how good it made me feel to
have the hand of brotherhood extended to me in those young impressionable
years. I will always have a special place in my heart for Eel River Lodge No. 147
of Fortuna because of this experience over thirty-five years ago. And what great
pleasure it gave me to revisit that Lodge this past August when your Grand
Lodge Officers took part in the observance of their one hundred and twcntyfifth anniversary.
I cite these experiences, because these are the experiences that have
helped make Masonry real and personal to me, so that later, when the occasion
did arise for me to become more actively involved in my Lodge, I welcomed it
as an opportunity. But let me say this in all sincerity, that even if I had never become a Grand Lodge Officer, even if I had not received any of the hono rs and

You know, it is not too hard to find answers to that question. You hear
it all the time. In my associations over the years with some of our concordant
bodies, I hear that question answered all the time. It always begins with the
phrase, "If Grand Lodge would only," and then follows a whole litany of "solutions", such as (a) eliminate the waiting period (b) be more up-to-date on the
liquor question (c) not require so much memorization (d) eliminate the
proficiency requirement to apply for concordant degrees (e) any other number
of personal biases about our fraternity.
Let's look at a couple of things. The waiting period and proficiency requirements were added to our Masonic law during our period of greatest and
most spectacular growth. Many Lodges were not only conferring degrees on a
w~ekly basis, but in some instances on a twice weekly basis; new Lodges were
bemg formed, and Masonry was enjoying great growth. National magazines,
such as Time ran feature articles on the Masonic order. However, in the midst
of this membership prosperity, concern began to grow that our lodges were becoming, in the academic jargon, merely degree mills, conferring degrees, but
not really making men into Masons. Many of those, it would seem, who were
recipients of degrees during lhat "golden age" were happy to accept the benefits
and privileges of Masonry, but were either ignorant of, or reluctant to accept,
the burdens and responsibilities of their membership. I had an experience not
too long ago that is illustrative of this. We had a new family move in next door
to us. The man had been seriously disabled in an industrial accident, but had
received a substantial settlement, so they were financially comfortable. They
were good neighbors, quiet, well-behaved, and sociable. In conversation it
developed that the man was a Mason. I invited him to go to Lodge with me, but
he indicated that his health would not permit him to sit for any extended period
o~ time, and this was true. As the months passed, his health steadily deteriorated,
with frequent stays in the hospital. He was, in effect living on borrowed time,
and eventually passed away. Both as a neighbor, and I thought, as a brother
Mason, we offered to help. The discussion of a Masonic service came up, and
the widow told me how much her husband's Masonic membership had meant
to him, and she was sure that he would want Masonic services. I told her that if
she would let me see her husband's dues card, I would have our Lodge Secretary
contact his Lodge and we would make the arrangements. There was no dues
card to be found, but she did locate his apron, which had his Lodge name on it.
When his Lodge, back in the midwest was contacted, they reported that he had
been suspended for non-payment of dues in 1%1, over twenty years earlier. Apparently after moving to California in 1959, he had ceased to pay his dues and

225

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

let himself be suspended. Yet, as I have already pointed out, he represented
himself as a Mason, and had told me that he had participated in the Masonic
Club in the large industrial concern where he had worked in Southern California. It was a sad experience for me to go back and tell my grieving neighbor th~t
her husband could not have Masonic services. It was also difficult for the fanuly to see that it was his own shortcomings that had produced this unfortunate
set of circumstances.

segment of our society. With the decline of the general moral tone of the country
that has taken place over the last several decades, it has become popular to
ridicule and regard as base hypocrites those individuals who profess to believe
in such principles as brotherly love, relief, and truth. In Masonry the word
"square" has a deep and profound meaning; it implies a devotion to duty, a sense
of fair play to one's fellow man, a commitment, as best one can, to square one's
actions by the square of virtue. However, during the tumultuous 1960's the term
"square" took on a new and somewhat derogatory meaning. To be square meant
that you were "not with it"; you were not "hep"; that you rejected the hedonistic
"if it feels good, do it" philosophy of the day.

Unfortunately, there seem to be hundreds, perhaps even thousands of
men who were raised during that great membership surge of the 1940 's and
1950 's, who, although they may have continued to pay their dues, an~ to th~t
extent have maintained their membership, they have graced the Lodge with their
presence but a few times since they were raised. We did a great job of getting
men into Masonry, but how good a job did we do of getting Masonry into men?
As I have pointed out to you, our concern in this regard caused us to
seek some remedy, and we took steps to try and enhance the Masonic ~duca­
tion of our members by requiring the third degree proficiency before taking any
other Masonic related degrees or orders. In other words, we thought that
greater attention to ritual, more emphasis on what one might call our Masonic
catechism, would produce the desired result. Now before going further, let me
make it clear that few have a greater sense of devotion to our Masonic ritual
than I do. One cannot have served this Grand Lodge for nearly eight years as a
District Inspector without having a profound respect for our ritual. However,
my brethren, I remind you that the word ritualistic is ~~t a t~rm that gene~ally
carries with it a positive connotation. To many people 1t 1mphes an e~phas1s on
form, with perhaps too little attention to meaning. And perhaps we m Masonry have tended to regard ritual as an end in itself, rather than a means to an end.
Maybe rather than requiring more ritual recitation, perhaps we should have
given some emphasis to some of the other asp~cts of Masonry, some of the _"burdens and responsibilities" that are a part of this great bro~herhood. Wh~t if l~e
Master bad called several of these newly made brethren with a message like this;
"Brother Smith, one of our fifty-year members passed away last evening. Woul.d
you, as one of our newest members, join with me in calling on his widow this
evening?" Or perhaps, some means could be take~ to. get these new me~bers
actively involved in calling on those who are hospitalized, who are shut-m, or
who can no longer drive to get to the meetings. I would venture to say that every
Lodge in this jurisdiction has members who have never made a sick call to a
brother or have never attended a Masonic funeral, let alone made calls on a
bereav;d family. Perhaps involving our brethren in these kinds of activities
would help to revive the sagging spirit of fraternalism. I heartily applaud the
positive step taken by our Grand Master this y~ar when he urge~ eac~ Lod.ge
to form a calling committee to try and re-establish fraternal rclationships with
those brethren whose attendance and other forms of fraternal contact have become rare and infrequent. Let's stop worrying about getting men into Masonry
and begin concentrating on getting Masonry into men!
We have to realistically accept the possibility that it may be a long time
before the principles espoused by Freemasonry once again appeal to a large

Out of these changes in our society, out of this atmosphere of permissiveness, a growing pressure has become evident that we too, must make some
changes. The large number of resolutions presented at these last two annual
communications is indicative of a sense of restlessness in our fraternity. Up until
a few years ago, one might say that the Grand Lodge of California, thanks to
the 5/6th requirement, was guided by the words of Viscount Falkland, who back
in 1641, stated, "When it is not necessary to change, it is necessary not to change."
But one can sense a growing sentiment that we do need to make some changes.
As such conviction begins to pervade our thinking, it is time to sound a word of
caution. First of all we must avoid falling into the trap that all change is good,
and that change for change's sake bas merit of its own. The second trap that we
need to avoid is the snare that tells us we need to make changes in Masonry to
bring us into conformity with the standards and mores of society. The test which
should be applied to proposed changes in Masonry, should always be the principles of FreemasoQry, which are based upon eternal truth. If we make changes
in our legislation on the liquor question, for example (and I do not know when
writing this whether this issue will be voted on before or after I speak) such
change should not be on the basis that social drinking is more prevalent in our
society today, but rather on the question of whether the cardinal virtue of
temperence is an individual or a Lodge responsibility. If we begin making changes in Masonry just to make us more attractive to 01.1r society, it would be a
perilous course to follow. Let me illustrate my point. We are all familiar with
the third "I will not" in our Master Mason obligation, which places certain
restrictions on our behavior. We live in an age of great sexual permissiveness,
in which the traditional standards of sexual morality seem to be observed more
in breach than in observance. How easy it would be to argue that, in order to
bring our fraternity more in step with society, we need to modify this portion of
our obligation. I submit to you, my brethren, that changes must be tested by our
ancient landmarks and principles.
Masons, at least for the past several decades, represent a diminishing
minority of our society and population. Our memberhip figures attest to that. It
is indisputable. However, we must be careful in attempting to remedy the situation, that we do not "throw out the baby with the bath water". We hope the day
will come when our society will return to the basic principles of morality that it
once shared with Freemasonry. It may not happen in our lifetime, but our job
is to keep the principles of Masonry alive, not to compromise them away in a
futile attempt to make the institution more popular. Masonry has faced mem-

PROCEED INGS OF THE

GRAND WOGE OF CALIFOR NIA

bership crises before in its history. In the aftermath of the Morgan affair, the
number of Lodges in New York State dropped from 227 to 41, and in Vermont
not a single Lodge remained in existence. In Nazi Germany, Masonry was ruthlessly suppressed , and its members persecuted , and Masonic communic ation
totally ceased. Masonry recovered from the slanderous attacks upon it associated with the Morgan affair. It recovered from the ruthless suppressio n of
dictatorships. It recovered because those members who remained, adhered to
the basic principles of Freemasonry, and by their individual adherence, continued to deserve the admiration and respect of their fellow citizens.

REPORT OF COMMI TIEE ON FINANCE

The question that faces us today is not persecutio n and suppressio n.
We know from our past history that Masonry can survive ruthless attacks from
without. Our enemy today is apathy, indifference and internal demoraliza tion.
But Masonry will survive because its principles are eternal, and as long as there
are a few good men, a few stout hearted men, to fan the sparks the flame will
not die out.
Our Father, by whose servants,
Our house was built of old,
Whose hand hath crowned her,
With blessings manifold
For thine unfailing mercies,
Far strewn along the way
With all who passed before us
We praise thy name today.
The change-ful years unresting,
Their silent course have sped,
New comrades ever bringing
In comrades steps to tread:
And some are long forgotten,
Long spent their hopes and fears
Safe rest they in thy keeping
Who changest not with years.
They reap not where they labored.
We reap what they have sown,
Our harvest may be garnered
By ages yet unknown,
The days of old have dowered us
With gifts beyond all praise
Oh, Father make us faithful,
To serve the coming days.

than $40,000.00 of the total. In spite of these averages, the total expense was under
budget by $52,380.00 and the Grand Master and the Committee s are to again be
com.mended for their efforts in holding down expenses. A detailed list of all expenditures can be found in the Grand Treasurer' s report.

business shall remain at $.18 per mile until the Annual Communic aiton in 1989.

Treasurer' s report to highlight part of the problem of the financing of Grand Lodge.

year, including his Annual Communic ation. Accountab ility has been difficult in the

REPORT OF THE CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
PUBLICATION BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
A Board consisting of the Grand Master, Grand Secretary, such other advisors as
may be necessary, and an Editor-in-Chief, appointed by the Grand Master, administer
the quarterly editing and mailing of the California Freemason, an official publication
of the Grand Lodge.
More than twenty million copies of the magazine have been distributed to the
members of the Jurisdiction, other Grand Lodges, and paid subscribers since its
founding 35 years ago.
Keeping the members of Lodges in California and Hawaii fully informed about
Masonic relations and activities is the primary purpose of the magazine. It reports on
the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic Foundation, California
Memorial Temple, the Masonic Youth Orders and other Masonic ventures throughout
the Jurisdiction and the world.

In addition to describing hundreds of Lodge events: Laymen's Nights, Hiram
Awards, Golden Veterans' Awards and Widow's Nights, the magazine promotes U.S.
Constitution and Public Schools Observances and is now focusing on Freemasonry's
support of drug and alcohol abuse educational programs in the public schools.
In the Spring of 1988 the California Freemason changed to a full size magazine
format, making it more readable, a better forum for articles, and saving several
thousand dollars of printing expense in the process.

REPORT OF THE MASONIC EDUCATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
The true tragedy of Freemasonry has been the steady decline in membership of
this most beneficient of organizations, Freemasonry. How can it be that a large
organization of men of highest moral and charitable character, dedicated to making
good men better, and having only the finest of motives, has been losing members faster
than it has been gaining members? Our one big problem is that, becuase our Brethren
do not know enough about Freemasonry, they can not and thus do not, speak up for

239

We the members of your Committee on Masonic Education, are dedicated to the
task of ~using the education of every Mason and Candidate in the Grand Jurisdiction
to the point where every one of them becomes a strong, proud proponent of
Freemasonry, ready to speak knowledgeably on the subject on any occassion.
COUNSELORS' PROGRAM
This year we have worked toward the development and activation of a progr~ of
education for Candidates based on a combination of an excellent booklet of readings
to be read to the Candidates and an organization of capable Brethren to cause the
program to occur.
Th.e booklet of readings is "The Lodge System of Masonic Information for Candidates", a reprinting, with permission, from the Grand Lodge of South Carolina; and
the organizational system is copied from the Counselors' ProSI:am of the <?rand ~ge
of Wisconsin. The booklet has been under study and a draft mcorporatmg add1t1ons
bas been reviewed by members of the Committee, then the Grand Master and the
Executive Committee, and the Grand Secretary. Publication, which is pending the
completion, review and revision of an additional chapter, on the subject of "The
Structure of Freemasonry: Grand Lodge and You", should occur in 1989.
The Counselors' drganization is made up of District Counselors, responsible for
Masonic Education in the Masonic Districts; Lodge Counselors, appointed by the
Lodge Masters, and responsible for Masonic Education in the Lodges; and
Candidates' Counselors, responsible for providing guidance and assistance ~o the
individual Candidates. To date, our Committee members have located and nommated
District Counselors for 118 of the 158 Masonic Districts, and letters of appointment
have been sent to all of them. Training of these District Counselors is being provided
by members of our Committee.

or area basis, and other short programs.

REPORT OF THE MASONIC HISTORY COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&. A.M. of California:
The History Committee is continuing to gather the individual histories of the
constituent Lodges; with the thought of eventually publishing them in a book. Special
emphasis has been put, this year, on the histories of the many extinct Lodges in the
latter half of the nineteenth century. Brother William Poynter, a member of the
Committee, has spent many hours examining records in the Grand Lodge Library
pertaining to these Lodges in order to make them as complete as possible.

REPORT OF THE INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of Califomia:
The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reporting annually to Grand
Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and those of its entities.

During the year quarterly meetings are held by the Committee with its investment
counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical firm reviews the performance
of the various funds as compared with similar funds, ie., endowment, non-profit and
trUSl funds, in the United States.
The primary concern of the Committee is the preservation of the principal of the
various funds together with the highest rate of return commensurate with safety and
good investment practice.
Three funds, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes General Fund

and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Fund constitute 96% of the total investments.
Among other funds supervised by the Committee are the General Fund of Grand
Lodge, the funds of California Masonic Memorial Temple, California Masonic Foundation and Amaranth, Pooled Income and thirteen restricted-use funds of Masonic
Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1988 was $207,298,000 com-

pared to $211,026,000 a year earlier, a decrease of 1.8%. The 1987-1988 cash yield from
the total invested funds was 7.2%.

Faced income securities including government and corporate bonds composed
50.8% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common stocks and cash
equivalents.

'

The Pooled lnrome Fund is of particular importance to the Masonic Homes. On
June 30, 1988, the Fund had a market value of $3,185,707. The cash yield was 8.8%.
The Pooled Income F11Dd gives Masons and others in California and Hawaii the
opportunity to create a lifetime income for themselves and for one-time designated
beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages may accrue to the contributor. Eventually, the
Masonic Homes becomes the final beneficiary.
The rewarding accumulation of as.sets in the various funds of Grand Lodge has
been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends. The operations of the
Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are almost entirely financed through the
income from Endowment and General Fund investments. The current expansion at
Union City is being funded entirely from the Hugo M. Lorber Fund. Other revenues
furnish support for the charitable activities and educational grants of the Grand Lodge
of California.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Funds investments rank among the highest in quality because the Investment
Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their management. The cash
yield and total return have been satisfactory in light of the Committee's conservative
investment policy and the volatility of securities markets.
Respectfully submitted,
H. Herbert P. Wilkins, Chairman

We have loaned 165 books which have been returned, and 2 are on indefinite loan
to specific individuals to be returned at the close of their office tenure. Purchases of a
number of books have been made, and included are Demott's Freemasonry in Americma
Culture and Society, Huss's The Master Builders, Quaruor Coronatorum, Vol. 98 and
MacLeish's Care of Antiques and Historical Collections. We have received donations
of 134 books, 28 from Myrl Hurley which includes a 7 volume set of beautifully
documented Masonic and Masonic-related stamps. We are, indeed, grateful to
Brother Hurley for his wonderful gifts to the Library and Museum. Additionally, 5
valuable and rare books were rebound as part of our maintenance program. We
continue to review the non-Masonic books and expect to have an accurate count of our
Library books at the close of next year.
The Museum collection has been enhanced by 70 donations, among which are a
Dudley watch from Alonzo Scull, in the name of his father, Clyde Scull; a 7 piece silver
English tea set that belonged to Randolph V. Whiting, Grand Master of California in
1934, donated by his niece, Elizabeth Goree; a silver trowel and wooden holder from
the cornerstone laying of the College of Physicians and Surgeons in 189<1 from Paradise
Lodge; and a pencil and color drawing of a Masonic parade crossing California Street
in 1984, donated by the artist, A. Robert Preston.
William Kludjian, Library and Museum Committeeman , has appraised 200
Museum artifacts, including several valuable pieces of jewelry. The appraisals were
completed during the two visits Brother Kludjian made during this fiscal year, one in
the week of Annual Communication , 1987 and the second in January 1988. We are very
fortunate to have Brother Kludjian who is a qualified appraiser and donates his time
and expertise without fee for the benefit of the Museum.
We have begun the arduous task of inventorying and cataloging the Museum
collections starting with Masonic aprons. To date we have cataloged 452 aprons, and
52 of the most fragile have been color photographed. The cost of photographing was
defrayed by an anonymous donor. To maintain the integrity of the aprons, another
Library and Museum Committeeman , Larry West, has donated his time, talent and all
materials in making wooden storage boxes for the aprons, which will provide protection
for this valuable collection.
At the behest of Most Worshipful Leo B. Mark, a public relations program was
initiated in which 1, 075 Library and Museum brochures and book lists were distributed
by Library Staff and Committeemen working with Inspectors, at various Masonic
functions throughout the year. Next year we plan to add a "New Books List" to distribute
with our present materials. Additionally, Brother Kludjian wrote an article, "Further
Light", published in the California Freemason, June 1988, Summer Quarter, Vol. 35,
No. 3 to inform new Brethren or Library services and to remind continuing members
of this excellent study resource.
The Library and Museum Committee gives special commendation to our loyal and
devoted Volunteers who are: Ironton Daube, Henry de Coursey, Bernie Katz, Irvin
Mintz, Orestes Matteoni, David Shull, George Sneddon, Jack Taylor, Louis Wells and
Larry West. We would be remiss if we did not express our thanks to the Grand
Secretary, Robert Klinger, and his staff; Loren Stritenberger, Masonic Memorial

REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of Califomia:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit its Annual
Report on the ~perations and conditions of the seventeen Masonic Service Bureaus
for the year ending June 30, 1988. The Committee is in its 61st year.
.. Right Worshipful Stan_ley L. Channon, D~puty. Grand Master, "."as appointed
liaison officer to the Comrmttee and we appreciate his support and assistance during
the year.

'"!is

Committee.is well aware ?fits r~ponsibility in overseeing and directing the
~ration of th.e va_rious Bureaus ma uniform manner. The Service Bureaus assist
SOJourners, their widows and orphans; operate blood banks; arrange and conduct
funerals for deceasc:d Masons; ~a~e inve~tigations; assist in processing applications
f~ the two Masoruc Aomes; VlSlt the sick and promote fraternal relations with
50Journers.
EXECUTIVE SECRETARIES
F?ur new Executive Secretaries were selected during the year as follows: Amie
Aseraon replaced ~aul Porter in the East Bay Bureau; Harry Dunlavy took William
E. Wharton s place in the Fresno Bureau; E. Charles Lamberson took over the Long
Beach Bureau from Robert J. MacDonald and Norman E. Royce took over the reins
of the Southern Alameda County Bureau from Emory E. Mumford. We wish these
Brcthre~ w~U in t~eir new assignments and o ur best wishes go to the outgoing Executive
Seaetaries in therr future endeavors.

MEETINGS
The Committee held four meetings during the year. One, which was held on the

first day of Grand Lodge week, Monday, October 12, permitted members of the various

Bureaus and Lodge Officers to contact the Committee and to receive help with the
many problems applicable to their areas.

A regional meeting was held in Oakland on February 7, 1988 with Committee

~mbers and 13 members and guests of the Bureaus from Northern California were

ID attendance. We were also pleased to have Very Worshipful Robert A

Grand Secretary, in attendance as the guest speaker.

Klinger

·

'

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND WOGE OF CALIFORNIA

A regional meeting was held in Los Angeles on March 26, 1988 with three
Committee members and 31 members and guests from Southern California Bureaus
attending. Chairman Ivie was pleased to introduce Worshipful Delmer W. May,
President of the Santa Barbara Bureau, former Committee Chairman and current
Advisor to the Committee. We were again pleased to have Very Worshipful Robert A.
Klinger, Grand Secretary, as our guest speaker.

OPERATING EXPENSES
Total cost for operating the seventeen Bureaus for the year ending June 30, 1988
amounted to $161,076.83. Fixed expenses were $98,094.64; telephone, printing and
postage were $11,468.02 and taxes were $7,2Tl.70. Some Executive Secretaries receive
a modest salary while others receive no salary. A few choose to receive mileage only.

On Wednesday, June 8, 1988, four members of the Committee met in Pasadena to
review the proposed budgets of the seventeen Masonic Service Bureaus. The Commit.
tee also reviewed its own budget for the 1988-1989 Masonic year. Also sitting in on the
meeting was Most Worshipful Roy J. Henville, Past Grand Master, and a member of
the ad hoc Committee to study the feasibility of establishing employment referral
services in some or all of the Masonic Service Bureaus in California. The Pasadena
Scottish Rite graciously provided the facilities for our meeting.

CONCLUSION S

252

After each of the above meeting.s a short business meeting of the Committee was
held to discuss items of immediate import.
TAXES
All Bureaus filed the required information with the Internal Revenue Service on
Form 990 and with the State Franchise Tax Board on either Form 199 or 199B. The
Los Angeles Bureau uses forms other than the 990 and 199. All Bureaus required to
file tax returns did so and filed them on time.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF FUND
The Bush Masonic Relief provides operating funds for the five Bureaus located
in the greater Los Angeles area. The contributions from this fund amounted to more
than 63% of the total income for the seventeen Bureaus and we appreciate this
generous contnbution for operations in the greater Los Angeles area.
Several of our Bureaus operate blood banks for the benefit of California Masons
and their families as well as for sojourners. 611 units of blood were donated during the
year and 306 units were released to provide this important life support to our members,
their families and to sojourners. In addition, $5,413.00 in cash ("green blood") was
donated to the San Francisco Bureau and $70.00 to the Fresno Bureau in lieu of actual
blood donations.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL IN LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A .M. of California:
A renewed general interest in Masonic endeavors, especially by young people,
women and foreign visitors, highlighted this year's annual report to the Grand Lodge.
The historic, two-story Temple, at 416-1/2 North Main Street, is an integral part
of the pioneer Garnier building. It adjoins the Pico House built in 1870 and was at the
tiJDe, one of the most elegant structures in the frontier town. These buildings comprise
an area well-known as El Pueblo de Los Angeles Historic Park. The city's first church,
first firehouse, first theater and the first Masonic Temple are situated here.
Since the 1984 Olympics, more emphasis has been placed by Old Plaza authorities
to attract more visitors, local and out-of-state. Daily, hundreds of tourists visit the
numerous buildings and shops in the Olvera Street grouping. Conducted two hour
tours of the Central City are given the first and third Wednesday of each month. Guides
point out the highlights as the tour begins in front of the Old Masonic Hall. The
"welcome" sign is o ut, and visitors to the Museum and Meeting Place find new delights
in inspecting Masonic artifacts and literature.
The Temple is open to the public on Tuesday through Friday from 10:00 A.M. to
3:00 P.M. A curator greets the visitors and cordially receives the guests. Appropriate
taped music fills the Temple as visitors tour the building. An average of 20 visitors,
mostly from G ermany, South America, France and Mexico "sign-in" during the week.
Busloads of children from summer schools, "Y" camps and on cross-country tours,

swarm in the Temple ~d pellet the curator with questions.
N
....
oo.

~
.....
~

So far this year, three women's organizations have expressed a desire to visit the
Temple on Saturday morning. We accommodate them and the curator presents a
comprehensive lecture on the development of Masonry, with emphasis of its origin in
California .
A number of television shows have been filmed in the Old Plaza area because of
the authentic locations of pioneer buildings and landmarks. The Historical Park
Committee has high hopes of finding several tenants to utilize the cho ice rebuilt area
of the Garnier building and Pico House. In time, this will become one of the favorite
tourist attractions in greater Los Angeles.

!
=

The Old Masonic Temple is the only area that is open. It was originally constructed
in 1858 and is the fourth two-story building in the city. From 1858 to 1884, Los Angeles
Lodge No. 42 met there. Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814 meets on Thursday.
Other Lodges and concerned Bodies may rent the Temple facilities. Rent for Lodges
is $45.00 per night. Youth groups are charged $25.00 for Saturday morning meetings.
Lodges desiring to rent the Hall should contact the Temple custodian at (213)626-4933
during museum hours.
